## §2 — Strategic position and what this design is for

## 2. Strategic position and what this design is for

This section owns the strategic case: why the rework exists, what territory PDD is taking, which surface it is taken on, and what counts as winning. It owns no geometry, no type scale, no palette hex, no field list, no deck size and no measurement window. Where a decision here has a numeric consequence, the number lives with the section that owns it and is cited, not copied. That discipline is the point: the first draft of this document broke because twelve sections each re-derived the same constants.

### 2.1 Why this rework exists

Three facts define the problem. Every code reference below was re-verified against `~/pdd-aggregator` on 17 Sep 2026.

**The pipeline has stopped.** The research digest reports `carousel_posts` holding 12 rows in total, spanning 2026-06-29 to 2026-07-03 (DB read in-session; not re-verified in this pass — the Supabase key is not available here). Today is 2026-09-17, so that is 76 days dark.

The filesystem corroborates it, and corrects a detail. `plan.mjs:23` names each archive folder with the date of the run that *archived* it, not the run it contains — so folder names are offset by one run, and `selection.json` is the truth. Five archived runs survive, plus the live directory; these are the last three:

| Folder | `selection.json` date | Contents | `publish.json` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `archive/2026-07-10-39463994` | planned 2026-07-02 | 7 slides, captions, `reel.mp4`, `story.mp4`, `cover.jpg` | **present**, `"date":"2026-07-03"` |
| `archive/2026-07-14-35175563` | planned 2026-07-10 | 7 slides, `CAPTION.txt`, `FB_CAPTION.txt`, `reel.mp4`, `story.mp4`, `cover.jpg` | **absent** |
| `~/Desktop/pdd-today` (live) | planned 2026-07-14 | 7 slides, `CAPTION.txt`, `FB_CAPTION.txt` — **no video assets, no `cover.jpg`** | **absent** |

So two runs after the last publish built decks and were never published. The 2026-07-10 run got all the way through carousel, reel and story and stopped at publish. The 2026-07-14 run stopped earlier, after the carousel build, before the reel and story ran. Neither crashed — each left a clean, complete set of artefacts for the stage it reached, and the pattern holds across the older archives too: `archive/2026-07-03-82818675` carries an earlier `publish.json` dated 2026-07-02, and `archive/2026-07-03-82897954` stopped at the plan stage with a shot list and reference JPEGs and no `out/` at all. The digest reports both Composio connections (Instagram and Facebook) active; the configured IG user id is `27332554436394910` and the FB Page id `1106603652538117` (`config.json:3-4`). Nothing in the plumbing is stopping a post.

**What we can and cannot conclude from that.** The artefacts establish that the routine stopped at the human approval gate. They do not establish *why*. "Somebody looked at it and refused to publish" and "nobody ran the routine that day" leave identical traces. Both explanations point at the same design conclusion — the manual gate is where this pipeline dies — so the rework does not need to resolve which it was. But the stronger claim should not be asserted.

**The template is not distribution-eligible on its own merits.** Instagram's Recommendation Guidelines (help.instagram.com/313829416281232, OFFICIAL) exclude "unoriginal content that is largely repurposed from another source with only minor, immaterial edits, without adding material value", and hold recommendations to a higher standard than Community Standards. A daily auto-generated deck built from other operators' photographs and other operators' prize data sits directly inside that exclusion. PDD's added value — the ticket cap and the odds it implies, the price, the closing date, the comparison across draws — must be visibly on the slide, not in the caption and not in the bio. Today it is not: `render.mjs:67` renders the odds as a trailing fragment of the closing-date line —

```js
<div class="closes"><b>${esc(d.closes)}</b>${d.odds ? ` · ${esc(d.odds)}` : ""}</div>
```

— and `.closes` is 33px (`styles.css:358`) beneath a 98px `.prize` (`styles.css:346`). The one datum no operator publishes is set at roughly one third the size of the datum every operator shows. 18 of 28 `font-size` declarations in `styles.css` are ≤46px (re-counted 17 Sep 2026). Those figures describe the shipped template; they are not spec values, and the replacement type scale is §3.5's alone.

**The template does not say what PDD is.** The cover headline is a per-category constant — six strings, "WIN A DREAM CAR" through "WIN RARE FINDS" (`config.json:16-53`) — rendered as the largest element on the slide (`build.mjs:140`, `render.mjs:150`). Unmapped categories fall through to the literal string `"WIN BIG"` (`config.mjs:15`), which the visual research names as an American-giveaway tell to strip. *(Shipped state only: the six `hook` constants and the `WIN BIG` fall-through are retired by §10.6a and physically removed from `config.json` by §8.7's migration, which is also the sole owner of the post-migration category schema and of `catCfg`'s fall-back behaviour. §2 states neither the retirement's mechanism nor any config value.)* The operator's name is fetched (`select.mjs:13-14`, `operators(name)`) and then dropped: `toDrawSlide()` (`format.mjs:55-66`) carries price, title, cash alternative, closing date, odds, image and slug, and no operator. Neither caption names an operator either (`caption.mjs:11-21`, `caption.mjs:27-36`). A viewer sees an operator's photograph, an operator-style headline and no indication that PDD is a third party rating anyone.

So the rework exists because the account is a poster pretending to be an operator, on a surface where being an operator is hopeless, at a moment when nobody is publishing it anyway.

### 2.2 The landscape, and why "third" is both true and modest

Every figure below was read directly from the live profile by an agent driving a headless browser on 17 Sep 2026 (MEASURED, single-day, single-observer census).

| Segment | Account | Followers |
|---|---|---|
| Operator | BOTB | 1,300,000 |
| Operator | 7days Performance | 304,000 |
| Operator | Omaze UK | 290,000 |
| Operator | Elite Competitions | 167,000 |
| Operator | Dream Car Giveaways | 137,000 |
| Operator | Good Life+ | 124,000 |
| Operator | Click Competitions | 106,000 |
| Operator | Rev Comps | 94,000 |
| **Directory** | Di Coke / SuperLucky | **12,100** |
| **Directory** | ThePrizeFinder | **770** |
| **Directory** | **PrizeDrawsDaily** | **66** |
| **Directory** | Competition Showroom | **47** |
| **Directory** | CompWatch | **2** |
| **Directory** | FindCompetitions | **0** |

Storm Competitions is age-gated and was not viewable; Bounty Competitions is private at 94; Loquax is private at 0; no genuine UK brand account was found for Raffle House. Carry that incompleteness forward.

The eight viewable operator accounts total 2,522,000 followers. The whole directory category totals 12,985, of which 12,100 belong to one person. Operators hold roughly 194× the directory category's aggregate following. Excluding Di Coke, every prize-draw directory in Britain totals 885 followers.

PDD at 66 is third in its category. That is a real position and a modest one. Second place is +704 followers away. First place is +12,034 away and belongs to a named human being, not a brand. **The only competitive milestone in this category within reach of an account at 66 is ThePrizeFinder's 770.** Di Coke is not the target; she is evidence about a lever (see 2.7).

The strategic reading: PDD is not fighting for share of a crowded feed. The directory category has effectively abandoned Instagram, and the surface is unoccupied. The competitive question is not "how do we out-post Omaze" — 290,000 against 66, with a product to sell and photographs of cars to sell it with. The question is whether the honest-directory position has a visual language at all. Nobody has built one.

### 2.3 The unoccupied territory is PDD's actual differentiator

The teardown ranked eight unoccupied positions. Four are committed to here — #1 LIGHT ground, #2 the scoreboard rather than the poster, #5 numerals as the only ornament, #6 showing the math — and #3 (naming a loser) is committed to as a *reserved render state* rather than an editorial programme. All five share one property that makes them strategically load-bearing rather than merely available:

**They are all outputs of having a database and no draws to sell.** The teardown's reasoning, which we adopt: an operator cannot run them. A light ground is unavailable to operators because they need dark to make glow work. A scoreboard is unavailable because a scoreboard implies comparison and comparison implies a rival. A negative verdict is unavailable because the verdict would be on themselves. And #6 is structurally closed to them: their job is to make odds feel small, and PDD's job is to make odds legible.

This is where the argument closes. The thing that makes PDD visually unoccupied is the same thing that makes it distribution-eligible. Putting the ticket cap, the odds, the price and the closing date at the top of the visual hierarchy is simultaneously the answer to Meta's "material value" exclusion and the answer to "what does a directory look like". Strategy and compliance converge rather than compete. So does the UK register: the public-infrastructure idiom (Kinneir/Calvert, British Rail, GOV.UK — calm, colour-as-meaning, numbers over adjectives) is the same register as the honest directory, so "purely UK vibe" and "trustworthy" converge too.

**#5 is a claim about ornament, not about category identity.** "Numerals as the only ornament" means no decorative artwork competing with the figures; it does not mean every deck looks identical. Per-category identity exists, and §8 is its sole owner — what it is, which surfaces carry it, how much ink it may spend and how it degrades on an unthemed category. §2 states only the constraint it imposes: category identity may not be carried by a second field of decorative marks that competes with, or could be mistaken for, the odds device.

**The signature device carries a known hole.** The odds dot grid — one dot per ticket in the cap, with the marked ticket shown only when every ticket in the cap is on the card — has been rendered once, as a mockup at a cap of 699, and an operator cannot copy it without damaging its own conversion. Two caveats travel with that, and §2 carries them rather than laundering them: the mockup's cell size is not the geometry §4 has since specified (§4.4's own residual risk is that *nothing at the ruled geometry has ever been rendered*), and the mockup file the spec cites for it is not present anywhere in `~/pdd-aggregator` as of 17 Sep 2026, so this section cannot verify the artefact independently and reports it as §4's and §5.8's evidence, not its own. Meanwhile real inventory routinely exceeds the grid's capacity: the deck published 2026-07-03 carries `Kamado Big Joe Grill · £3 · 1 in 9,999` in its own caption (`archive/2026-07-10-39463994/out/CAPTION.txt:8`).

§4.7 owns the ceiling, the above-ceiling encoding and the marker rule; §4.4 owns the lattice, the count-slide vertical budget and the surface assignment, and is now the single normative source for all of them — §4's earlier pair of incompatible answers has been collapsed to one, and §5.7's competing table is deleted. §2 takes no position on any of those values. One strategic observation survives the settlement, which is why it belongs here: **the full band remains a minority event.** The settled ceiling excludes most live caps, so on most draws the device renders as a numeral with a clipped band rather than as a complete picture of the cap; §5.8 measures coverage at roughly one draw in four at the settled ceiling. The differentiator therefore rests on the odds *figure's* hierarchy — largest text element, tabular mono, above the prize name — at least as much as on the picture, and the picture is a bonus that lands on a minority of draws. That is a materially smaller claim than "the dot grid is the signature", and it should be stated in those terms to the product owner rather than discovered later.

**The corollary is a firm exclusion.** PDD must not look like an operator, and the confirmed clichés are the operator's uniform: dark ground with gold or orange glow, flying banknotes, retail-sticker vocabulary, HH:MM:SS countdown pills, chrome bevelled numerals, the vanity stat band, inherited operator artwork. The current cover runs most of them. The decorative-layer inventory of that cover is §1.5 A7's and is not restated here. One correction is handed to §1 rather than published as a competing count: re-read on 17 Sep 2026, `bgFx(rays = true, …)` at `render.mjs:43-44` expands to `.bloom` + `.rays` + the particle field, so A7's single "particles" row is three layers — which is why §2's old count of seven and A7's six disagreed. The cover stack is emitted at `render.mjs:143-158`; §1.5 A7 states its contents, and §3.8's deletion list should be reconciled against whatever count A7 settles on.

**One compliance defect inherited from the current template must not survive.** Every slide's footer reads `18+ · UK ONLY · PLAY RESPONSIBLY`, rendered at four sites — `render.mjs:69`, `:122`, `:157` and `:172` — so this is four edits, not one (`.footer .rp` at 19px, `styles.css:367`). *(An earlier draft of this section cited `:68` and `:121`; both were off by one and are corrected here.)* A fifth instance sits outside the frame, in the Facebook caption at `caption.mjs:35`; that one is §10.6's to remove, not §2's. Prize competitions and free draws sit outside Gambling Act 2005 licensing, so the operative code is CAP Section 8, not 16 or 17; dressing the template in gambling language is inaccurate and re-categorises PDD in the viewer's mind. That categorisation argument is §2's and is the reason the line goes. **What replaces it is not §2's to write.** The conditions band — its field list, its exact strings, its type contract, its per-surface geometry, the free-entry state and the age mark — is §10.2's, and the banned-wording list and its enforcement are §10.6/§10.6a's. §2 states no legal line, no character budget and no band height, and neither should any other section outside §10.

We accept one cost of the direction openly: the light newsprint register (§3.2's tokens; hexes are §3's) deliberately diverges from prizedrawsdaily.co.uk, which is dark plus orange. Social and site will not match. That is a decision, not an oversight (see risks).

### 2.4 Why the carousel is the primary growth surface

The benchmark evidence (Socialinsider, 35M posts across 447,613 accounts, Jan–Dec 2025, published 20 Feb 2026, MEASURED) gives median **views** by format in the 1–5K follower tier:

| Format | Median views, 1–5K tier | Ratio to carousel |
|---|---|---|
| Carousel | 993 | 1.00 |
| Reel | 580 | 0.58 |
| Image | 417 | 0.42 |

Carousels **out-view** reels by roughly 1.7× at this size, and the study reports the advantage holding in every band. That is a views figure, not a reach figure, and it is never restated as reach anywhere in this spec (§12.4; §11.5 mandate 5; §11.6 trap 1 — views count replays, reach does not, and this spec's success criteria are reach-denominated).

**Carry the caveat.** PDD is at 66 followers. The lowest band the study reports is 1–5K, so 993 is not a forecast for this account and must never be quoted as a target. What transfers is the *ordering*, and even the ordering is a median across hundreds of thousands of accounts, not a promise for one niche UK account with 66 followers and 76 days of silence behind it.

Four structural reasons reinforce the ordering, independent of the benchmark:

1. **The reel has a harder entry gate.** Skip rate in the 1–5K tier is 65.50% within the first three seconds (Socialinsider, 140K reels, Jan–Jun 2026, MEASURED). The Reels Chaining system card (transparency.meta.com, updated 11 Nov 2025, OFFICIAL) discloses an abandonment head and watch duration measured relative to peer reels of similar length, so a reel is judged inside its own cohort. PDD has no measured ability to win that cohort.
2. **The reel cannot be A/B tested here.** Trial Reels require a public professional account with 200 followers (help.instagram.com/1013292530224018, OFFICIAL). PDD is at 66. The platform's own test rig is unavailable until +134 followers.
3. **The carousel has a mechanism the reel does not.** Mosseri (Oct 2024, OFFICIAL) states that when a viewer does not swipe, Instagram "will often give that carousel a second chance and automatically move to that second piece of media". A carousel gets two shots at the same impression.
4. **The carousel is the cheaper surface to change.** Stills render PNGs from headless Chromium via Playwright (`render.mjs`, 9,757 bytes, `chromium.launch()` at `render.mjs:186`) plus `styles.css`. The video path is `reel-template.mjs` (57,082 bytes — the largest file in `carousel/`), `reel.mjs` (16,416) and `story.mjs` (16,305), and it is currently broken against Meta's safe area. The full element-by-element table is §12.4's and §1.5 B's; the correct summary, which supersedes the digest's phrasing, is that **nothing in the current Reel is fully inside Derived Safe Box A — `.pcard` breaches it on all four edges** (the per-edge breach deltas are §12.4's and are not restated here; `reel-template.mjs:178` sets `left:64px; right:64px; top:240px; height:950px`, re-verified 17 Sep 2026). The price, the deadline chip, the CTA, the handle and the compliance footer have all been rendering underneath Instagram's own interface. The reel needs more repair for less benchmarked return.

There is also a design argument, stated as design judgement rather than evidence: the product is a list of tonight's draws, and a list is natively a carousel. A reel has to narrate a list; a carousel *is* one.

**Deck size is a lever, not a fixed seven, and it is §5.11's to set.** Today's deck is `[intro, ...5 draws, cta]` = 7 slides (`build.mjs:150`, `plan.mjs:10`) — a description of what ships, not a spec value. Eden's slide-count dataset (655,385 carousels / 12,159 creators, Aug 2025–Aug 2026) puts breakout rate at ~27% for 6 slides, 28.8% at 10 and 32.1% at 14, plateauing around 18–20. **Caveat carried: Eden sells a carousel generator, so "more slides win" is commercially convenient, and breakout-versus-own-median may be confounded by effort. Treat the direction as credible and the magnitude as soft.** §2 rules only that seven is not sacred, that the direction may be acted on and the magnitude may not be quoted as a threshold, and that "5–8 slides is optimal" — uncited folklore contradicted by the only real dataset — is not used. The constant itself, the backup count, the degradation ladder and the minimum viable deck are §5.11's.

One correction to a claim this section previously made: **raw inventory does not settle the lever.** The digest records 899 enterable draws with an image and a ticket cap, cash-prizes alone holding 351, and that is ample in aggregate — but the binding quantity is per-category rows surviving the fetch cap at `select.mjs:20` (`limit=300`), the recent-slug exclusion window, and §10.4's eligibility predicate. §5.11 records that thin categories can fall below its pool bar. "Inventory does not constrain the lever" was true of the total and false of the constraint that actually binds. (The total itself is unstable across the document — 880, 897 and 899 all appear in different sections, none re-verified in this pass; whoever locks a figure should query it once and cite the query.)

### 2.5 The format risk, stated honestly

**No UK operator or aggregator runs a daily multi-draw roundup carousel.** In this genre a carousel means "more angles of one prize". PDD's format is genre-unprecedented, which is simultaneously the only uncontested position available and a real comprehension risk: a viewer who has learned the convention may read slide 1 as a single prize and slides 2–6 as more photographs of it. If that happens, the comparison — the entire point — never lands, and the deck reads as a repetitive single-prize post.

The closest template match found anywhere is Wowcher's "Wow Week": a dated, named, week-long daily roundup carousel with three deals per post, a circular dark price badge top-right on inner slides only, and no prices on the cover. That is evidence the shape can work commercially in the UK. **It is a single template match, from a deals retailer with an established audience, not a validated pattern in the prize-draw genre.** Do not read it as more than an existence proof.

This section does not design the mitigation. It fixes four requirements the rest of the spec must satisfy, because they exist to answer this risk specifically:

- **The count must be the cover's claim.** The cover must state how many draws are inside, at the scale of a headline, and the count must be generated from the deck that actually rendered rather than from a constant. The exact string and its wording law are §10.6a's; the cover layout is §5.4's; the deck-size constant it interpolates is §5.11's. Today the count appears three times and never at hero scale: inside `.intro-kicker` at 30px via the banner (`build.mjs:139`; `styles.css:469-470`), inside `.intro-sub` at 31px as "N TO WIN" (`render.mjs:140,152`; `styles.css:478`), and inside the swipe line (`render.mjs:155`) — all sitting behind a category constant at hero scale. Those sizes are shipped values, not spec values.
- **Slide 2 must be independently intelligible** — carrying brand mark, recency, the premise and a standalone fact — because of Mosseri's second-chance behaviour. §5.6 is the owner of slide 2's content. Its ruling satisfies brand, recency, premise and fact, and drops the day-angle kicker in favour of the count. §2 accepts that trade and records it as a residual risk rather than re-opening it: the slide served cold now states what PDD is and what the day's sharpest number is, but not what the day's angle is.
- **The swipe cue must be a numbered counter plus a partial element bleeding across the slide edge, not an arrow.** NN/g finds arrows signify tapping and are ignored, and Instagram already draws its own multi-image icon and pagination dots. `render.mjs:155` currently ships exactly the wrong cue: `SWIPE TO SEE ALL${d.count ? " " + esc(d.count) : ""} →`.
- **Inner slides must be distinguishable from one another at thumbnail size**, and the differentiator must be the data, not the photo treatment. With the full odds band a minority event under §4's settled ceiling, the load falls on the prize name, the price and the digit count of the odds figure. That is in direct tension with normalising scraped operator assets to a uniform crop and background (§9), which makes slides look *more* alike. Naming the tension here; the resolution belongs to §5 and §9.

**Comprehension itself is not measurable.** There is no swipe-through rate, no per-slide insight, no exit rate and no completion metric for carousels — not in the Graph API and not in the app; carousel children carry no individual insights, only the parent album does. We therefore design against this risk and measure only its downstream effects. Any success criterion that implies per-slide behaviour is inadmissible, on this surface and on §8's per-category scenes alike.

### 2.6 What winning looks like

Winning is that PDD becomes the only UK account publishing a dated, checkable scoreboard of tonight's draws, every day, without interruption, in a visual language no operator can adopt — and that the format earns distribution on the value it shows rather than on the photographs it borrows.

**§11.7 is the governing measurement framework.** It owns the instrumentation gate (G1), the coarse "did it do anything" criterion (A1), the per-post criteria (B1–B10), every baseline, every window and the kill rule; §11.5 owns denominators. §2 previously published a second, competing set of six criteria on a different calendar with a different denominator. That table is deleted. Nothing in this section states a measurement window, a target multiple or a rate. Where an earlier draft of §2 said "S1", read §11.7's continuity gate; where it said "S3", read §11.7 B1, which is per-post reach at `t72` and not the account-level series §2 previously nominated — §11.5 mandate 1 bans the denominator §2 was using, and §11.7 B1 records that zero per-post reach rows exist today.

Two things remain §2's to state, because they are strategic commitments rather than measurements.

**First: continuity outranks aesthetics, and the boundary against compliance is now defined.** A design that does not get published has failed regardless of how it looks. That principle previously produced a rule — "never fail the build" — which contradicted §5.3 and §10.8 outright. The contradiction is resolved, not by weakening either side, but by moving the common failure out of the build:

- **Eligibility is a selection predicate, not a render gate.** A draw without fresh, sourced, renderable provenance for its ticket cap is never selected (§10.4). It cannot be dropped at render, cannot collapse a slot, cannot consume a backup and cannot escalate a run. The first run therefore does not hard-fail; it draws from a smaller, evidenced pool.
- **Per-row failures at build time degrade the deck; they do not kill the run.** A draw that fails at the model stage is dropped and a backup promoted, then the deck shrinks one draw at a time (§5.11, §10.8 class B).
- **A hard fail is reserved for genuine invariant breaks** — §10.8's class A list, which includes a missing or undersized conditions band, a wording ban hit, absent alt text and a verdict claim on an unevidenced figure — and for a deck that cannot reach §5.11's floor. On those, compliance wins and the run exits non-zero. A no-publish day that exits zero is worse than one that exits non-zero, because it is indistinguishable from success.

**No warn-and-render flag.** An unstamped ticket cap may be a sold count, a per-person cap or a neighbouring competition's number, and all three understate the denominator and flatter the odds — the one direction of error this device exists to be immune to. §10.4 refuses the flag and §2 endorses that refusal: a staged rollout that publishes an unevidenced odds claim is not a staged rollout, it is the breach.

**Second: the continuity clock starts after the schema work, not before it.** The provenance columns, the parser change that records which extraction tier produced a cap, and the write-path fix that re-stamps an unchanged cap do not exist today. §12.4's Stage 0 is blocking and §12.3's scope exclusion has been narrowed to admit it — recording provenance about a figure the scraper already reads is a derivation over work already done, not scraper-accuracy work. Until Stage 0 ships and one full daily sweep re-stamps the reachable inventory, the odds device cannot render lawfully at any geometry, and a continuity streak begun before that is a streak of posts that may not be publishable. **The clock starts at Stage 0's exit criterion, which §12.4 owns.** This is the single largest sequencing dependency in the document and it belongs in §2's statement of winning because it determines when winning can begin to be counted.

**What is explicitly not a success criterion, and why:**

- **Swipe-through rate** — the metric does not exist, in the API or the app. The commonly cited "15–25% is good" is unmeasurable folklore.
- **Per-slide drop-off** — same reason. This also rules out measuring §8's per-category scenes: there is no per-slide, per-child or skip-rate signal to attribute them with.
- **Engagement rate against the "~10%" benchmark** — fabricated. And the honest figure is not a follower-denominated one either: per §11.5, engagement is reported against per-post reach at `t72`, and any external benchmark quoted alongside it must carry its own denominator.
- **Reach parity with operators** — 194× the aggregate following. Not a game worth scoring.
- **Facebook performance** — Buffer's 0–1K tier median reach is 30 per post (52M+ posts, updated 13 Sep 2026), Instagram out-reaches Facebook at every measured page size, and the Page's published state is unverified. Facebook is a cross-post destination, not a design surface or a yardstick.
- **Trending audio** — closed by construction: the Content Publishing API has no parameter to attach Instagram library music, so audio must be baked into the MP4.

**The attribution contract, restated so it no longer conflicts with the Reel.** PDD must be visibly a third party naming the operator. That is discharged differently per surface and the split is deliberate: the operator's **name** on the carousel draw slide (§5.13's lockup); the operator's **entry host** in the conditions band on every surface including the Reel and the Story (§10.2 — this is also how CAP 8.17's how-to-participate condition is discharged, and it is why a generic "enter on operator site" phrase is not sufficient); the operator's **@handle** in the caption only. §2 previously made operator identity a binary per-slide precondition, which §6 could not satisfy within its own time budget and which §10.2 has since discharged by other means. The Reel is therefore exempt from carrying an operator *name* on the frame, and that exemption is written down here rather than left as a silent divergence.

### 2.7 The lever we are choosing not to pull

The clearest natural experiment in this category is Di Coke at 12,100 against every faceless directory at under 800: **a face works**. We are not building on it.

The reason previously given was effort arithmetic: a daily shoot stacks a heavy manual step on an approval gate already proven fragile "at zero marginal effort". **The premise of that argument no longer holds and must be corrected.** The pipeline was never effortless — `carousel/DAILY.md` is explicit that the routine is trigger-based ("say **publish today**"), that it "shows you one composite preview, and posts on your OK", and that "your daily job is basically *approve*" (`DAILY.md:4,6-7`), and `plan.mjs:67` already writes a `SHOTLIST.txt` inviting the operator to drop in their own photographs. The rework as specified adds more recurring manual work on top: §9.7's Tier-3 review of candidate images against normalised masters, §10.8's `out/COMPLIANCE.txt` triage, §11.2's weekly hand-transcription of the retention curve and skip rate with an archived screenshot, a daily authored caption, and the publish approval. The marginal effort is not zero and never was, and nothing in the document totals it. That total is a real scope item and it is handed to §12 as a named requirement: a per-day and per-week operator time budget, itemised by step, with a stated ceiling, because the failure mode that killed this pipeline twice is the human gate and the only defence is counting the minutes before they accumulate.

The rejection survives the correction, on two grounds that do not depend on the "zero effort" premise:

1. **The increment is still strictly larger.** Shoot, review and re-shoot is a per-day cost of a different order from approving a preview or triaging a compliance file, and it is the one step that cannot be automated later. Every other item above can be folded, batched or dropped; a daily presenter cannot.
2. **It is a different product.** Di Coke is a long-tenured personality brand, not a directory product launched cold, so "a face works" and "an established comping personality works" are not separable from this data. A face makes PDD a person who recommends draws; the position this design takes is an institution that publishes them. The second is the one no operator can copy.

So the design bets on the lever automation is actually good at — numbers, dates and provenance rendered precisely, at scale, every night — and accepts that this lever has no comparable evidence behind it in this category. That is a genuine trade, and it is recorded in the risks rather than argued away. If §12's minute budget comes back above its ceiling, the correct response is to cut the added manual steps, not to revisit the presenter, because the presenter is rejected on product grounds as well as on effort.

### Decisions this section commits to
- The Instagram carousel is the primary growth surface for this rework. Reel and Story are secondary and are not the yardstick against which the redesign is judged. The supporting benchmark is a **views** figure (carousel 993 / reel 580, 1–5K tier) and is never restated as reach (§12.4, §11.5, §11.6).
- Added material value — the ticket cap and the odds it implies, the ticket price and the closing date, rendered visibly on the slide — is a distribution-eligibility requirement under Instagram's Recommendation Guidelines, not an aesthetic preference.
- Eligibility is enforced by EXCLUDING an ineligible draw from SELECTION, per §10.4's predicate. §2 makes no claim that the odds device is a render-time binary precondition, and no claim that the build never fails.
- Continuity outranks aesthetics, and its boundary against compliance is: selection predicate first (§10.4), then class-B draw-drop, backup promotion and one-draw-at-a-time deck shrink (§5.11, §10.8), then class-A hard fail for genuine invariant breaks and for a deck below §5.11's floor. Compliance wins at the point of failure; continuity is protected by making the common failures non-fatal, not by disabling the fatal ones.
- No warn-and-render flag for unevidenced ticket caps. §2 endorses §10.4's refusal: an unstamped cap can understate the denominator, which is the one direction of error the device exists to be immune to.
- The continuity clock starts at §12.4's Stage 0 exit criterion. §12.3's scope exclusion is narrowed to admit the provenance columns, the extraction-method enum and the write-path fix, because recording provenance about a figure already read is a derivation, not scraper-accuracy work.
- §11.7 is the governing measurement framework and §11.5 owns denominators. §2's former S1–S6 table is deleted; this section states no measurement window, no target multiple and no rate.
- The design targets unoccupied territories #1 (light ground), #2 (scoreboard not poster), #5 (numerals as the only ornament) and #6 (showing the math), because each is an output of holding a database and selling no draws, and is therefore structurally closed to operators.
- #5 constrains ornament, not category identity. §8 owns per-category identity on every surface; §2's only constraint is that it may not be carried by a second field of marks that competes with or could be mistaken for the odds device.
- The odds device is the signature, and the full dot band is a minority event under §4's settled ceiling. §4.7 owns the ceiling, the above-ceiling encoding and the marker rule; §4.4 owns the lattice, the count-slide budget and the surface assignment. §2 states no ceiling, no band width, no origin and no fallback encoding, and records that the differentiator now rests principally on the odds figure's hierarchy, with the grid as a minority bonus.
- The one rendered proof of the device is a mockup at a cap of 699, at a cell size that is not the ruled geometry, and the file is not present in `~/pdd-aggregator` as of 17 Sep 2026. §2 reports it as §4's and §5.8's evidence and does not treat the device as proven at the specified geometry.
- Territory #3 (naming a loser) is committed to as a reserved render state: the verdict element must be able to render a negative state. The caution colour and the grounds it is legible on are §3.2's and §10.5's — it is a paper-ground colour and is not available on rail blue. The editorial calendar for negative verdicts is out of scope here.
- The social register is light newsprint with rail-blue standing chrome (tokens and hexes are §3's) and deliberately diverges from prizedrawsdaily.co.uk's dark-plus-orange identity, because light is the one ground operators structurally cannot occupy.
- 'PLAY RESPONSIBLY' is removed. Prize competitions sit under CAP Section 8, not 16/17; gambling furniture is inaccurate and re-categorises PDD. It renders at four sites (`render.mjs:69`, `:122`, `:157`, `:172` — verified 17 Sep 2026; an earlier draft's `:68`/`:121` were off by one), so this is four edits, plus a fifth instance in the Facebook caption at `caption.mjs:35` that belongs to §10.6. What replaces it — the conditions band's fields, strings, type and geometry — is §10.2's; the wording law is §10.6/§10.6a's. §2 states no legal line and no band height.
- Attribution is discharged per surface: operator name on the carousel draw slide (§5.13), operator entry host in the conditions band on every surface including the Reel and Story (§10.2), @handle in the caption. The Reel is explicitly exempt from carrying the operator name on the frame; `format.mjs:55-66` still drops the name `select.mjs:13-14` fetches, and `caption.mjs` (11-21, 27-36) still builds no mention.
- Deck size is a lever, not fixed at seven (`build.mjs:150`, `plan.mjs:10`), and §5.11 is its normative owner. §2 rules only that the Eden direction may be acted on, that its magnitude may not be quoted as a threshold, and that '5–8 slides is optimal' is unsourced and unused.
- Raw inventory does not settle deck size. The binding quantity is per-category rows surviving the 300-row fetch cap (`select.mjs:20`), the recent-slug exclusion and §10.4's predicate — §5.11's constraint, not the 899-draw total, which is itself unstable across sections (880 / 897 / 899).
- The swipe cue is a numbered counter plus a bleeding element crossing the slide edge. The arrow label at `render.mjs:155` is removed.
- Slide 2 is designed as a second cover, independently intelligible on brand, recency, premise and a standalone fact, because Instagram gives an unswiped carousel a second chance on the second item. §5.6 owns its content, and §2 accepts its trade of the day-angle kicker for the count.
- The cover's decorative-layer inventory is §1.5 A7's and is cited, not restated. One correction is handed to §1: `bgFx(rays = true, …)` at `render.mjs:43-44` expands to `.bloom` + `.rays` + particles, so the 'particles' row is three layers.
- The six per-category `hook` constants and the `WIN BIG` fall-through are retired by §10.6a and removed from `config.json` by §8.7's migration. §2 cites them only as shipped state and publishes no config key, value or fall-back behaviour.
- The correct statement of the Reel's safe-area defect is §12.4's: nothing in the current Reel is fully inside Derived Safe Box A, and `.pcard` breaches it on all four edges. The per-edge deltas are §12.4's and are no longer restated here; the digest's 'everything except `.pcard`' phrasing is not repeated.
- The competitive milestone is ThePrizeFinder at 770 (+704), not Di Coke at 12,100.
- Facebook is a cross-post destination, not a design surface, and does not contribute to the success criteria for this rework.
- A daily on-camera presenter is rejected on two grounds that survive the correction to §2.7's premise: the increment of shoot/review/re-shoot is strictly larger than any other manual step and cannot be automated later, and a face makes PDD a person who recommends draws rather than an institution that publishes them. The effort argument alone no longer carries the rejection, because the pipeline was already attended (`DAILY.md:4,6-7`, `plan.mjs:67`) and the rework adds recurring manual work that nothing in this document totals.
- §12 must carry a per-day and per-week operator time budget, itemised by step, with a stated ceiling. The dormancy was a human-gate failure and operator minutes are the one cost the document never counts.

### Open questions
- Does the Composio Graph pull return per-media reach for Instagram carousels? `insights.mjs:36-42` hard-codes `media_id:'account'`, so post-level reach attribution is unproven, and §11.7 B1 — the criterion that replaced §2's account-level one — cannot be computed without it. This is now §11's blocker, recorded here because §2's statement of winning depends on it.
- Does the same pull return `views` for carousel media? The 993/580/417 benchmark is denominated in views and the pipeline ingests none, so PDD's numbers are not directly comparable to the benchmark until this is resolved.
- Are saves and shares retrievable for Instagram carousels through the Composio pull? The digest establishes only that the pipeline does not ingest them, not that the API withholds them. If available they are the strongest proxy for a roundup being kept for later.
- Is Instagram referral traffic to prizedrawsdaily.co.uk attributable in the site's analytics? The site repo is out of scope and the wiring is unverified here. If it is not attributable, the commercial outcome is unmeasurable and judgement stops at reach, interactions and followers.
- Is the Facebook Page (id `1106603652538117`, `config.json:4`) unpublished because it was never published, or because Meta unpublished it? The digest records `is_published:false` from an agent reading the live Page via Composio and flags it as not independently verified. The owner must confirm in Meta Business Suite before Facebook is reasoned about further.
- Does a daily deck stay single-category (today's `pickBestCategory` behaviour, `select.mjs:27-51`) or mix categories? `config.json:10` already carries a cross-category series name, "TONIGHT'S UK DRAWS", while the cover renders a per-category constant — an existing incoherence. This changes what the cover can honestly claim and which comprehension mitigation applies, and it interacts with §5.11's category-rotation risk.
- Does the product owner accept the deliberate divergence between the light social register and the dark site, and is there an intention to bring the site across later or to keep them separate permanently?
- Does the product owner accept that the full dot grid renders on a minority of draws, with the marked ticket rarer still? If cross-slide comparison of grid height matters more than the photograph, the answer is a §5 decision (delete the photograph from every draw slide) that §2 has not taken on the owner's behalf.

*Closed since the previous draft:* the free-entry route question is now §10.2's (`draws.free_entry_route`, a Stage 0 column with a lawful `unknown` state) and §12.4's Stage 0 sequencing — §2's original evidence for raising it stands and is worth carrying into §10: no free-entry field exists in the columns `select.mjs:13-14` fetches, and a repo grep finds free-postal-entry text only inside a scraped test fixture. The unthemed-category question is now §8's, whose scene set covers the live taxonomy and whose NEUTRAL scene is the honest fall-through; the config side of it is closed by §8.7's migration, which authors the two missing categories so the taxonomy and the config carry the same eight slugs and the `WIN BIG` fall-through no longer exists — the category counts and weights are §8.7's and are not restated here. The §4 band question is closed: §4.4 is the single normative owner of the lattice, the count-slide budget and the surface assignment, and §4.7 of the ceiling and the marker. The `ig_reach` metric-key question (`insights.mjs:40` stores `entry.name || "reach"`, so a field rename silently breaks the series) moves to §11 with the account series it belongs to.

### Risks
- The Socialinsider follower bands start at 1–5K and PDD is at 66, below the lowest measured band. The carousel-over-reel ordering may not hold for a cold 66-follower account, and 993 is not a forecast. If §11.7's format comparison does not reproduce the ordering locally, the premise of this section is wrong and the reel deserves reconsideration.
- The roundup carousel is genre-unprecedented in UK prize draws, and comprehension cannot be measured. If viewers read the deck as more angles of one prize, the failure appears only as flat reach with no diagnostic signal telling us why.
- **The differentiator is thinner than §2 originally claimed.** Under §4's settled ceiling the band is clipped on most live caps and the marked ticket disappears above it, so on many days — and on a car-draws deck, plausibly every day — the device renders as a numeral and a clipped grid. The odds figure's hierarchy still discharges the material-value argument; the *picture* that made the position uncopyable is a minority event. This is the single largest reduction in scope of §2's strategic claim.
- **Nothing at the ruled geometry has ever been rendered**, and the one artefact the spec cites as proof — a mockup at a cap of 699 — is at a different cell size and is not present in `~/pdd-aggregator` as of 17 Sep 2026. Every claim in this document about how the device reads is a claim about something nobody has looked at.
- Slide 2 now carries the count rather than the day's angle (§5.6). It is the slide Instagram serves cold on an unswiped carousel, and it states brand, recency, premise and one strong fact but no editorial angle. If cold-entry comprehension is the binding constraint, this is where it will show, and there is no metric that will tell us.
- Normalising scraped operator assets to a uniform crop and background (§9) works directly against making inner slides distinguishable at thumbnail size, and the rarity of the grid removes one of the differentiators that was supposed to compensate. The tension is real and its resolution sits with §5 and §9.
- The light register breaks visual continuity with prizedrawsdaily.co.uk. A viewer arriving from Instagram meets a differently-branded site, which costs recognition at exactly the moment the funnel depends on it.
- Eden's slide-count direction comes from a vendor selling a carousel generator and may be confounded by creator effort. If deck size is increased on that basis and breakout does not follow, the cost is per-deck render time and per-deck editorial load — which attacks continuity, the primary criterion.
- The only measured directory success in this category is a named human being with 12,100 followers, and that comparison is confounded by tenure and by her being a personality brand rather than a directory product. The design deliberately bets on data-as-ornament instead, a lever with no comparable evidence in this category and no fallback if it does not work.
- **The largest risk is not aesthetic.** If the rework improves the artefact but publishing still stops, nothing has been achieved. `DAILY.md:4,6-7` confirms the routine is trigger-based and approval-gated, so the failure mode is latent in the workflow, not in the design. The rework adds recurring manual work (§9.7, §10.8, §11.2, the daily caption) on top of that gate, and no section totals the minutes. Any design decision that raises per-day human effort is a cost against the primary criterion and should be argued as one.
- **The publish gate is a file check, not a publication control.** `publish.json` is not what reaches the platform — an agent session reads it and calls Composio tools, and §7.5 documents that agent already choosing a different tool than the runbook specified. Until §10.7's caption hash binding and post-publish reconciliation land, a compliance pass is a statement about a file on disk. §2 does not fix this; it records that the continuity criterion and the wording law both depend on a step neither of them currently controls.
- Meta enforces the Recommendation Guidelines opaquely. "Material value" has no published threshold, so the eligibility contract can only ever be a good-faith render-time commitment; we cannot verify eligibility except by observing whether reach moves.
- The landscape figures are a single-day, single-observer census taken on 2026-09-17. Storm Competitions was not viewable, no UK brand account was found for Raffle House, and Loquax and Bounty are private. Follower counts move; the ratios and the category-abandonment conclusion should be re-checked before any decision rests on them again.
- The `carousel_posts` row counts and date span are digest-reported from an in-session DB read and were NOT re-verified in this pass (no Supabase key available). The filesystem corroborates the 76-day gap and the two unpublished runs, but the 12-rows-across-5-days figure rests on a single unrepeated read. So does the 899-draw inventory total, which other sections state as 880 and 897.
- Metricool's mention finding (+108% reach, +167% comments for accounts under 2K) is correlational, not causal, and it is the basis for naming and tagging operators. Tagging an operator also creates a commercial relationship risk for a brand whose position is that it publishes negative verdicts.
- Archive folders under `~/Desktop/pdd-today/archive` are named by `plan.mjs:23` with the date of the run that archived them, not the run they contain, and `plan.mjs:27-30` prunes anything older than 14 days. Any future forensic claim about run history must read `selection.json` rather than the folder name. The five surviving archives are two months past that prune window and survive only because the prune runs inside `plan.mjs` and `plan.mjs` has not run since 14 Jul — the evidence exists *because* the pipeline is dead, and the first successful run will destroy most of it.
- The continuity clock cannot start until §12.4's Stage 0 ships, and Stage 0's exit criterion — enough evidenced draws in enough categories to fill a deck daily — has never been measured. If it comes back thin, the deck runs degraded every day while the config says otherwise, and the rework's first visible symptom is a shrinking post rather than a failing one.

- §2's own unthemed-category arithmetic (6 vs 8 categories, ~147 draws, ~16%) is retired; §8.7's migration authors the two missing categories and owns the counts.

**Open questions**

- The mockup file cited as the odds device's only rendered proof is not present under ~/pdd-aggregator; either path it or retire the 'proven at 1 in 699' claim across §4, §5.8 and §2.
- The 899 / 897 / 880 inventory-total divergence remains unresolved across §2, §5.11 and §8.5.

**Risks**

- §2.3's 'minority event' framing depends on §4 staying collapsed to one ruling; a reopened ceiling changes the reading though not the text, since §2 publishes no digit.
- §5.8's 'roughly one draw in four' coverage figure is now attributed to the settled ceiling but was measured against the higher of the two former ceilings; §5.8 should confirm it still holds.
- §2 no longer carries the `.pcard` deltas, so a reader of §2 alone cannot size the safe-area defect.
- The decorative-stack enumeration remains deleted on the assumption that §1.5 A7 carries it.
