**Open questions**

- Does the Reel mark get redrawn at ≤213.15px? This is new: §6.3 handed the decision to §8 with a ≤133.95px ceiling computed against the retired `CHECKED 09:00` stamp, and §10.4's shorter `READ 09:00` has moved it. M as drawn now misses by 6.85px, not 86px. Added to §8's open questions rather than decided here, because it is a scene-design call.
- Is the 4:5 draw-slide box correction consistent with §5.7's own scene-mount paragraph? C1 told §5.7 to state the photo well parametrically ('x 0 → sheet edge by its rendered height') and let §8 compute the area. §8 now computes the ORIGIN too, which §5.7 should not restate. Worth one line in §5.7 confirming it publishes no y-origin for the region.
- The 3% mean tone behind §6.3's published ≈0.59% painted-ink figure is roughly 2.5× the 1.18% mean the eight located scenes actually compute to. I flagged the assumption inside §8 rather than changing the figure, because §6.3 publishes it and §8 quotes it — but if §6 wants the honest number it is nearer 0.23%, and it strengthens the majority-text defence rather than weakening it.
- The count-slide 4:5 box now has two published values (y 132…432 at §5's 750px rect, y 132…437 re-derived against §4.4's ceiling) and a third and fourth at the clipped state and cap 99. §8 declares it a render-time computation, which is right, but no section says which value a FIXTURE renders at. G3 and G4 diff against a fixture; that fixture needs a stated cap.
- §8.5's gym row now reads 'No marking. The stripes stay', which is correct — but the sports variant table still has no row for the case where a deck mixes gym draws with golf draws, and the ground is resolved once per run from the DECK's category, not from the modal variant. That is fine for the ground (it is the category's, not the variant's) and I left it, but nobody has said what the mark does on a card whose draw matched nothing while the previous card's matched golf.

**Risks**

- The draw-slide box correction (632…867 → 697…932) depends on §4.4's column being read correctly: photo 565 → 20 → lockup 45 → 20 → prize 140 → 20 → E2 240 = 1,050 in a well of y 132…1182. I derived the origin from the C1 settlement's own arithmetic rather than from §4.4's file. If §4.4 orders those blocks differently — a gap before the photo, say — the origin shifts by that gap and y_c and the house crests shift with it. The HEIGHT (235) and the region AREA (241,645) are safe either way.
- The 65 × 48 corner strip at x 1015…1080, y 132…180 is a deduction from the published areas, not something any section states. It is the only term that makes all four subtractions close, so it is almost certainly real — but it means the draw slide's ground paints a 65px-wide, 48px-tall patch of category art in the top-right corner, detached from everything else, and nobody has looked at that. If §5 intends the sheet edge to start at y 132 rather than 180, the strip vanishes and all four region areas drop by 3,120 px².
- Fixing the mark-slot arithmetic to §6.3's measured wordmark makes M's failure smaller (6.85px, not 86px) and therefore more tempting to fix by shaving. The section keeps the suppress-never-shrink rule, but a reader who sees '6.85px short' will reach for the 22.5px §6.3 says removing the letter-spacing recovers, which is a §3.4 decision about the wordmark's face, not §8's.
- Nothing here is rendered, and the corrections are all arithmetic on arithmetic. The draw-slide origin moved 65px and no fixture exists to catch it being wrong again; the same class of stale-origin defect survived a gutter pass and a full settlement pass precisely because the AREA stayed constant while the coordinate did not. Until G3 runs against a real fixture, the only defence is that every box is now shown as a derivation with its sum beside it.

---

## §9 Asset normalisation at ingest — adversarially checked and corrected

## 9. Asset normalisation at ingest

Operator photography is the largest uncontrolled variable in the whole pipeline. Every other input — price, cap, close date, odds — arrives as a typed field with a known range. The photograph arrives as whatever the operator's marketing team made, and the template currently absorbs that variance at render time. This section specifies moving the absorption to ingest.

§9 is the normative owner of asset normalisation: the tiers, the masters, the resolution floors, the cache and the refusal ladder. No other section specifies them. Conversely, this section owns nothing about layout: the rects it serves belong to §5.7, §5.9, §6.2 and §7.2, the conditions-band wording belongs to §10.2, the figure-provenance contract belongs to §10.4, deck size belongs to §5.11, per-category visual identity belongs to §8, and this section states none of their values.

The research digest's own framing — that normalising asset complexity at ingest is "probably the highest-leverage single change available" — is the research's judgement, not a measured result, and is carried here as such. Nothing in this section claims a measured effect on reach; §9.14 explains why no such measurement is currently obtainable.

---

### 9.1 What happens today

**Fetch.** `carousel/fetchimg.mjs` drives a headless Chromium over each draw's `entry_url`, harvests `og:image` / `twitter:image`, JSON-LD `image`, every `<img>` (`currentSrc`, `srcset`, `data-src`, `data-large_image`, `data-zoom-image`), `<source srcset>` and any `<a href>` ending in an image extension (fetchimg.mjs:72-101), filters an explicit junk regex of theme/icon/payment/social assets (fetchimg.mjs:24), upgrades Shopify and WooCommerce URLs to full resolution (fetchimg.mjs:35-46), scores candidates — with a `+5_000_000` boost when the URL path contains a keyword from the prize title (fetchimg.mjs:119) — and downloads the top 5 into `~/Desktop/pdd-today/.fetched/{slug}/cand-1..N.<ext>`. `pick.txt` is written with candidate 1 as the default guess (fetchimg.mjs:197). VERIFIED: the fetch list is `[...sel.draws, ...(sel.backups || [])]` at fetchimg.mjs:170 with `perDraw = 5` at fetchimg.mjs:165, so backups are already pre-fetched and the candidate budget already scales with the deck.

**Selection.** `build.mjs:55-66` resolves each draw's hero in the order: a photo the user dropped in `pdd-today/` → the auto-fetched `pick.txt` → nothing. `reel.mjs:205-220` and `story.mjs:223-237` each re-implement the same resolution independently, including their own copies of the `minDimOk(auto, 500)` call.

**Absorption.** There is no normalisation stage. The template compensates:

| Compensation | Location | What it is hiding |
|---|---|---|
| `s.framePhotoContain = srcKind === "auto-fetched"` | build.mjs:117 | unknown incoming aspect ratio |
| `.card .photo.contain { padding: 40px }` | styles.css:320 | unknown subject margin |
| `.card .cbg img { object-fit: contain; transform: scale(1.5); filter: blur(40px) saturate(1.6) brightness(1.12); opacity: .55 }` | styles.css:313-314 | unknown background colour — filled with a blurred, saturation-boosted copy of the operator's own image |
| `.pcard .cbg img { object-fit: cover; scale(1.5); blur(40px) saturate(1.6) brightness(1.1) }` | reel-template.mjs:184-185 | **the same trick, second copy** |
| `.hf-bg img { object-fit: cover; blur(42px) saturate(1.55) }` | reel-template.mjs:168-169 and again reel.mjs:87-88 | **third and fourth copies** (reel scene backdrop; reel cover card) |
| `.st-card .cbg img { object-fit: cover; scale(1.5); blur(40px) saturate(1.6) }` | story.mjs:79-80 | **fifth copy** |
| `.thumb { border: 2px solid rgba(var(--ray-rgb),.7); background: radial-gradient(…); box-shadow: 0 12px 26px…, 0 0 22px…, inset 0 1px 0… }` | styles.css:399-402 | six mutually incompatible tiles held together by chrome |
| `.card .photo-grad { box-shadow: inset 0 0 90px rgba(0,0,0,.42); background: linear-gradient(180deg, transparent 58%, rgba(0,0,0,.42)) }` | styles.css:323-324 | unknown luminance at the bottom of the frame, where text sits |

The blurred-self backdrop is the clearest symptom, and it exists **five times across four files** — `styles.css`, `reel-template.mjs` (twice), `reel.mjs` and `story.mjs`. Only the `styles.css` copy is a stylesheet rule; the other four are string literals inside the video templates' own CSS, which the token-lift regex never touches (it matches only `:root` and `[data-theme="…"]` blocks — reel-template.mjs:46, story.mjs:31, reel.mjs:69). Its side effect is to import the operator's dominant colour into PDD's card. Under the approved newsprint direction it cannot survive anywhere. It can only be deleted once ingest guarantees a known ground — and it has to be deleted in all five places or the Reel and Story keep importing operator colour after the carousel has stopped.

**The existing gates, and their gaps.** Three thresholds exist, in two files, none of them on the short edge:

| Gate | Location | Rule | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Byte floor | fetchimg.mjs:153 | `buf.length > 3000` | a 3 KB file at 1600px is a flat colour or a denial graphic, not a photograph |
| Candidate floor | fetchimg.mjs:190-191 | drop `max(w,h) < 400`, but only once ≥2 candidates clear 400 | applies to candidates at fetch time only |
| Publish floor | imgcheck.mjs:33-38, called at build.mjs:63, reel.mjs:219, story.mjs:236 | `max(w,h) >= 500` | longest edge, so a 1600×200 banner strip passes; a QA-edited `pick.txt` pointing at a 450px candidate is silently demoted to a typographic card with only a console line (build.mjs:64) |

Two further defects found in-session:

1. `imgcheck.mjs:36` returns `true` for an undecodable buffer with the comment *"unknown format → let the render gate judge"*. The render gate does not judge resolution. `render.mjs:20-27` waits for `document.fonts.ready` and for every `<img>` to fire `load` or `error`; `render.mjs:191` then waits for `window.__ready`. Nothing inspects dimensions. Combined with `fetchimg.mjs:150`, which maps any unrecognised `image/*` content type to the extension `jpg`, an AVIF of any size is saved as `.jpg` and fails `dimsFromBuffer`. Precise consequence: because `fetchimg.mjs:190` also requires `d.dims` to be truthy, such a candidate is dropped *if at least two other candidates clear 400px* — but when it is one of the only one or two candidates it survives to `pick.txt` and then passes the 500px gate unconditionally. So the hole is narrow but real, and it opens exactly on the thin-candidate draws where the fallback matters most.
2. `fetchimg.mjs` has no block-page detection at all. It imports only `chromium`, `mkdir`, `workDir` and `dimsFromBuffer` (fetchimg.mjs:17-20). A refused page and a page with genuinely no product images both land in `.fetched/report.json` as `reason: "no candidates"` (fetchimg.mjs:195). The repo has already learned this lesson once on the JSON adapters — `extractor.mjs:43-60` documents a WAF challenge page being handed to the parser *as the product*, and `extractor.mjs:37` (`BLOCK_RE`) / `extractor.mjs:40` (`looksBlocked`) plus `probe.mjs:27` are the guards that resulted. The image path never got them.

---

### 9.2 The contract

A normalisation stage sits between fetch and the three renderers, as a module (`carousel/normalise.mjs`) that `build.mjs`, `reel.mjs` and `story.mjs` all consume — exactly as all three consume `pick.txt` today, and replacing the three independent `minDimOk(auto, 500)` calls (build.mjs:63, reel.mjs:219, story.mjs:236) with one. `pick.txt` becomes `pick.json`:

```
{ key, plate: { file, w, h } | null,
        cutout: { file, subjectPx } | null,
        eligible: { well, sheetEdge, reel, story },   // booleans, per §9.4
        rejected: [ { file, tier, reason } ] }
```

Three read sites change with it: build.mjs:47-53, reel.mjs:205-211, story.mjs:223-229. `contact.mjs:22`, which globs `cand-*` to build the QA sheet, gains the masters alongside (§9.8).

Its guarantee to the template, and the only guarantee the template may rely on:

> Every asset handed to a renderer is a photograph of the prize, on a known ground, within a known luminance band, with its subject inside a recorded bounding box, carrying no baked-in text and no third-party promotional furniture, and at a resolution that has been checked against **the specific rect that surface ships**. An asset that cannot meet this for a given surface is not handed to that surface.

**The contract deliberately does not promise a single aspect ratio.** The draft of this section did, and it was wrong: it stored one master "at the largest surface's exact geometry so nothing ever upscales downstream" and concluded "the widest aspect anything needs is 1.341:1". §9.3 shows the surviving surfaces need crops from 0.0958:1 to 3.48:1 — a 36:1 spread — so no stored shape can be every surface's shape. What removes the guessing is the **recorded subject box**, from which each surface derives its own crop deterministically, not a uniform file shape.

**It also no longer promises a typographic fallback.** `DAILY.md:57` currently says that where a draw's page is blocked or branded and no backup helps, the slide falls back to a clean typographic card. Under §9.4's ladder a refused asset becomes a §10.8 class-B drop entering §5.11's degradation ladder instead, so the typographic card survives only where §5 chooses to keep it as a layout state. That supersession is named here because the daily runbook still documents the old behaviour and will contradict the build otherwise.

The template stops guessing. Every compensation in the table above is then deletable, which is the point: the render-time absorption is not a cost worth paying twice, let alone five times.

---

### 9.3 What the masters must actually serve

The draft derived the master from `.card` (styles.css:306) and `.pcard` (reel-template.mjs:178) and from the cover thumbnail strip. All three are deleted by this spec — §6.2 deletes `.pcard` and takes the Reel photograph full-bleed, and §5.4/§5.15 delete the strip and `thumbsHtml()` (render.mjs:126-131 definition, render.mjs:153 call site). The derivation below is re-run against the surfaces the spec actually ships.

It is run at **shipped pixels** — what the platform receives — because that is what a resolution budget should be measured against. The carousel renders 1080×1350 CSS at `deviceScaleFactor: 2` (render.mjs:2, :187) but `publish.mjs:63` draws the 2160×2700 PNG onto a 1080×1350 canvas for upload, so the carousel's shipped pixel is its CSS pixel. The Reel and Story render at `deviceScaleFactor: 1` (reel.mjs:36, capture.mjs:12) and are not resampled.

| Consumer | Owner | Crop aspect | Shipped rect | Shipped rect if the optional 1440×1800 Facebook variant (§7.6) is taken |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reel + Reel cover, full-bleed photograph | §6.2 | 0.5625:1 | **1080 × 1920** | n/a |
| Carousel draw-slide photo well (x 0 → 1015) | §5.7 | 1015/h | 1015 × h | 1353 × 1.333h |
| Carousel sheet edge — the *next* draw's photograph | §5.9 | 0.0958:1 | 96 × 1002 (65 of the 96 land in frame) | 128 × 1336 |
| Story band 3 | §7.2 | §7.2's | 950 × h₃ | n/a |
| Facebook carousel | §7.6 | inherits the carousel PNG | 1080 × 1350 | 1440 × 1800 |

The photo well's height `h` is §5.7's to set and is not restated here; it is the flex residual §4.4 computes, and across the values now in play it runs from §5.7's own 500 px floor to 615 px, so the well's crop aspect runs **2.03:1 … 1.650:1**. §7.2's band 3 height `h₃` is likewise §7.2's, which sets it at 273 px in a 950 px band — **3.48:1**, the widest crop in the system, and §7.2 records that this is the arithmetic maximum the surface can give the photograph rather than a discretionary squeeze. **None of the floors below move with it**, because band 3's binding demand is its 950 px width, which is under the photo well's, and a shorter band takes less source height, not more. The sheet edge is the narrowest crop at 0.0958:1; the element is 96 px wide and 65 of those px land in frame (§3.5's gutter ruling puts §5.9's hairline at x 1015, so the strip runs x 1015 → 1111: 65 px on-frame, 31 px off), and the crop is prepared at the element's full 96 px because the off-frame 31 px is cropped by the canvas, not by us.

**The binding numbers fall out directly.** Across every subject-bearing crop the widest shipped width demanded is **1353 px** — the photo well, and only if §7.6's optional Facebook variant is taken; without that variant the widest is the **Reel's 1080 px**, since the well then ships at 1015. The tallest shipped height demanded is **1920 px** (the Reel). A rectangle containing all of them must therefore be at least 1353 × 1920 with the Facebook variant, 1080 × 1920 without it.

**The Reel is the binding consumer, and this is the headline change.** §6.3 owns the photograph's share of the Reel frame and puts it at no less than **71.563%** of every frame (546 px of expanded chrome out of 1920) and **86.406%** during the open window (261 px collapsed), and §6 states the consequence plainly: at that share during the open window, an ungraded collage IS the reel. Those constants are §6.3's and are carried here by reference, not restated as §9's; nothing in this section turns on their exact value, and §6.3's own caveat travels with them: the figure is an area calculation of opaque chrome, "my own construction", not a read of Instagram's classifier, since Meta publishes no threshold for "majority text". What is not in dispute is the geometry: a 9:16 frame at 1080 × 1920 with no card to hide a bad crop behind is a far harder ask of operator photography than the 952 × 950 `.pcard` it replaces, and the height floor it sets — 1920 px — is roughly four times the 500 px longest-edge rule it replaces.

**§6's crop constraint is accepted here.** §6 line 45 assigns the normaliser one job it cannot do after the fact: keep "the prize's identifying subject, and any burned-in text, clear of x 853 … 1080 × y 1152 … 1920" — the L-notch, 227 × 768 = 174,336 px², **8.41% of the frame**. §9.4 states the mechanism.

---

### 9.4 The two masters, and what each surface takes

Two derivatives, named for what they are rather than lettered. **The letters are retired** because §7.9 already uses "Class A" and "Class B" for Meta's prohibited and demoted engagement-bait tiers, on the same spec, and two unrelated Class-A/B taxonomies in one document is a defect waiting to happen.

**The plate — a photograph of a real scene, tone-normalised and subject-anchored.**
Stored as JPEG q90 on the source's own aspect, at the largest rectangle the source supplies within the 1.35× upscale budget, **capped at 1600 × 2000**. The cap is derived, not chosen: 1600 is what the Reel's L-notch pan allowance asks for (1536, below) rounded up, and it also clears the widest shipped width demand — the photo well's 1353 under §7.6's variant — by 247 px; 2000 clears the tallest shipped height, the Reel's 1920, by 80 px. Storing more is bytes nobody reads. The sidecar records the stored size, and every surface's eligibility is a comparison against it.

Worked crops from a full-size plate:
- Reel: scale 1600 × 2000 by 0.96 → 1536 × 1920, then crop 1080 wide, leaving **456 px of horizontal pan** in which to satisfy the L-notch rule below.
- Photo well at its widest case (2.03:1): 1600 × 788 taken from the plate, shipped at 1015 × 500 (×0.634) or 1353 × 667 (×0.846).
- Story band 3 at §7.2's 3.48:1: 1600 × 460, shipped at 950 × 273 (×0.594).
- Sheet edge (0.0958:1): 191.6 × 2000 (192 rounded), shipped at 96 × 1002 (×0.501) or 128 × 1336 (×0.668).

**The cutout — a product keyed off a near-uniform light ground.**
Stored as a 1200 × 1200 PNG with **alpha preserved and no ground baked in**, subject fitted to a centred 1100 × 1100 box, 2px feather. The draft baked §3's paper into the file; storing alpha instead is strictly better, because it lets the renderer composite onto whatever ground §3 and §8 put behind it rather than forcing paper at ingest, and it costs nothing. The measured source ground colour is recorded in the sidecar for audit.

Why the subject box stays at 1100 px: the largest shipped subject any cutout consumer asks for is 820 px (the photo well at its tallest, 615 CSS px, under §7.6's optional 1440 variant). 1100 gives 1.34× headroom, so a change to §5.7's well height or a future wider surface does not force a re-ingest, and the cost is one 1200 × 1200 PNG.

**Which master each surface takes.**

| Surface | Master | Anchoring |
|---|---|---|
| Carousel photo well (§5.7) | cutout if one exists, else plate | subject box centred in the crop |
| Carousel sheet edge (§5.9) | **plate only** | no subject anchor — a centre-column slice |
| Reel + Reel cover, full-bleed (§6.2) | **plate only** | subject box, panned to clear the L-notch |
| Story band 3 (§7.2) | cutout if one exists, else plate | subject box centred in the crop |

**The Reel never takes a cutout, and this closes an open hole.** A cutout on a full-bleed 9:16 frame is a subject on flat paper, and §6.3's guarantee that no frame of any reel is less than its photograph floor would then be discharged by paper. The arithmetic: the entire 1100 × 1100 subject *box* is 1,210,000 px² of a 2,073,600 px² frame — **58.4%** — and the keyed subject inside that box is smaller still. That is below §6.3's 71.563% photograph floor (1,483,970 px²) by a wide margin, and below every value that constant has ever been given, so the conclusion does not depend on its exact figure. The resolution is not to argue with §6.3 but to note that keying is PDD's choice, not a property of the file: a source that yields a cutout is a photograph, so it also yields a plate whenever it clears the plate floor, and the Reel takes that. The sheet edge takes the plate for the same class of reason — a 96 px slice of a cutout is usually pure paper, which destroys the "next sheet in the stack" cue §5.9 is buying.

**Resolution floors — replacing the `max(w,h) >= 500` rule.** The binding dimension is the source region around the recorded subject box, and the floor is expressed as the maximum upscale permitted, per surface family. Every hard floor is ⌈preferred ÷ 1.35⌉.

| Tier | Serves | Source region, no upscale | Hard floor (≤1.35× upscale) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **plate, full** | every surface, including the Reel and Reel cover | ≥ 1536 × 1920 — the Reel's 1080 shipped width plus the 456 px of L-notch pan, at its 1920 shipped height | ≥ 1138 × 1423 |
| **plate, still-only** | photo well, sheet edge, Story band 3 — not the Reel | ≥ 1015 × 1002 | ≥ 752 × 743 |
| **plate, still-only**, if §7.6's 1440×1800 Facebook variant is taken | same | ≥ 1353 × 1336 | ≥ 1003 × 990 |
| **cutout** | photo well, Story band 3 | subject short edge ≥ 1100 | ≥ 815 |
| **refuse** | — | — | below the still-only floor; or source aspect outside 1:3 … 3:1; or `dimsFromBuffer` returns null (**reversing imgcheck.mjs:36**) |

The full tier's preferred region is the Reel's demand **plus pan**, not its bare demand, and the difference matters: a source at exactly 1080 × 1920 needs no upscale at all but has zero horizontal slack, so the L-notch rule below can only be satisfied if the subject already sits clear. Such a source is tried at zero pan and refused to the still-only tier if no valid placement exists, rather than being failed on the width floor — otherwise a strictly better source (no upscale) would be rejected while a worse one (1.3× upscale from 1138 × 1423) passed.

1.35× is design judgement — the upscale a Lanczos resample survives at these viewing sizes. The 1:3…3:1 aspect rule is what kills the banner strip the current longest-edge gate passes. The floors are geometry-derived, not corpus-calibrated (open question 1), and they ship behind two env overrides, `ASSET_MIN_PLATE` and `ASSET_MIN_SUBJECT`, defaulting to the tabled values, so the measurement can retune them without a code change.

Note what the third row costs: §7.6's optional 1440×1800 Facebook variant is free in render terms but **raises the still-only floor by a third**, from 1015 × 1002 to 1353 × 1336. That is a real price on an upgrade §7.6 describes as free, and it is the kind of number that only appears when the floors are derived from shipped pixels.

**The L-notch rule.** For the Reel and Reel cover only: the 1080 × 1920 crop is valid if and only if neither the recorded subject box nor any text band the §9.7 pre-filter flagged intersects **x 853 … 1080 × y 1152 … 1920**. The normaliser pans the crop horizontally within the plate's available slack (456 px from a full-size plate) to find a valid placement and refuses the asset for the Reel if none exists. This is an intersection test, not a transform.

**One refusal ladder, and §9 asks for a backup last.** On a refusal the normaliser falls through in order: **next candidate → the operator's stored `image_url` → the still-only tier (if the failure was the Reel's floor alone) → refuse the asset**. Only when all four are exhausted does the draw become a §10.8 class-B drop entering §5.11's degradation ladder. §9 therefore consumes at most one backup per draw, and only when every candidate for that draw has failed. Stated because §5.11's pool now has several consumers and the order in which they draw on it is §5.11's to set; this is §9's undertaking to arrive at that pool last.

---

### 9.5 Tier 0 — admissibility (deterministic, no model)

Byte-level, unit-testable, free, and the only tier that may run unattended without a fallback path.

- **Magic-byte sniff** before trusting any content type, following the precedent at `fix-operator-logos.mjs:26-32` (JPEG `FF D8 FF`, PNG `89 50 4E 47`, GIF, RIFF/WebP, `ftypavif` at offset 4). That file's own comment records why: "Trustpilot serves real JPEG/AVIF as octet-stream, while a hotlink-blocked host serves an HTML error page with a 200."
- **Byte floor raised from 3000 to 8192.** A file that decodes to ≥1000px on the short edge and occupies under 8 KB is a flat colour, a gradient or a denial graphic. The threshold is design judgement.
- **Frame-entropy test, run on the trimmed region only.** Downsample to 64 × 64 **after trimming any near-uniform border ring** (the same ring measured in §9.6), quantise to 5 bits per channel, and refuse if distinct colours < 48 **or** the Shannon entropy of the luminance histogram < 3.0 bits. Trimming first is load-bearing: a legitimate white-studio product shot is mostly one colour and would fail a whole-frame test, which is precisely the cutout case this stage must not eat. Thresholds are design judgement.
- **Block-page propagation.** `fetchimg.mjs` adopts `looksBlocked()` (extractor.mjs:40) and `BLOCK_RE` (probe.mjs:27) against the fetched page text, and `.fetched/report.json` distinguishes `reason: "blocked"` from `reason: "no candidates"`. The memory rule stands: never score a block as "the site is down". Most HTML challenge pages are already excluded at `fetchimg.mjs:149-151` because the content type is not `image/*`; what remains is image-typed junk, which the byte and entropy tests catch. What the guard actually buys is **naming the cause** in the report, exactly as `extractor.mjs`'s two counters do.

---

### 9.6 Tier 1 — geometry, ground, tone (deterministic, no model)

**Ground detection.** Sample the 8px border ring of the decoded image and compute its luminance standard deviation and mean L*:

- **Ring σ < 6/255 and mean L\* > 88 — a product on a near-uniform light ground.** The ground is keyed out by luminance with a 2px feather and the subject is written to a cutout. No cutout model, no API, deterministic. A plate is written from the same source in the same pass whenever the plate floor is met.
- **Ring σ ≥ 6 — a photograph of a real scene.** Plate only, no cutout.
- **Composite (collage, info-card, branded tile).** Refused (§9.7).

Keeping a real photograph as a photograph rather than cutting it out is also the distribution-safe choice: Instagram's published ranking note (about.instagram.com, 31 May 2023) makes reels "less visible" when they are "majority text", and the photograph is what keeps PDD's frames from reading as text cards.

**No hairline, no inset.** The draft separated a photograph from the paper with "a 2px #D8D3C8 hairline with a 2% inset". That is deleted. §5.7 forbids it outright ("No card frame, no border, no glow, no podium"), §5.14 makes `#D8D3C8` decorative-only, and on the Reel the photograph is full-bleed to the canvas edge so the hairline could not exist there anyway — a border on one surface and not another is exactly the divergence this section exists to end. §9 does not carve an exception into another section's element.

What the hairline was actually solving is the edge of a light photograph dissolving into light paper, and that is handled inside the crop instead. §3's paper `#F7F5F0` is Y = 0.9137 (the value §8's ruling publishes), which is **L\* = 96.6**. So:

- **Global highlight guard:** 95th-percentile L\* ≤ 94 on the subject region (unchanged from the draft).
- **Edge guard, new:** on any shipped crop whose edge abuts §3's paper ground — the photo well's top and bottom bands, all four edges of Story band 3, and the sheet edge's left hairline — the 95th-percentile L\* of the outer 24px ring must be **≤ 92**, i.e. at least **4.6 L\* below the paper**. On the conventional ΔL\* ≈ 1 JND rule of thumb that is about 4.6 perceptible steps; the rule of thumb is a convention, not a measurement of these surfaces.

The edge guard is a **test, not a transform.** The crop search prefers an anchor whose edge rings pass; it never darkens pixels to force a pass, because a local darkening ramp is a vignette and §8.4 forbids one that resolves as an edge. If no anchor passes, the asset is admitted anyway and the sidecar records `edge_dissolves: true` with the measured value. The residual is then a named number rather than a silent softness, and the one-line remedy — a 1px `--rule` hairline on the well — remains available to §5.7 as §5's decision, not §9's.

**Tone normalisation.** Measured on the subject region only, on a 256px-long-edge downsample:

| Target | Value | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Mean luminance | L\* = 62 ± 4 | single gain + gamma pair |
| Shadow clip | 5th percentile L\* ≥ 8 | lift |
| Highlight clip | 95th percentile L\* ≤ 94 | pull |
| Contrast stretch | only if the 5–95 range < 55 L\* points | never more than 1.25× |
| Mean chroma | C\* ≤ 38 | desaturate only if measured C\* > 46, never below 0.8× original |

**The L\* 62 target is per-master, not global.** A genuinely dark prize photograph — a black car at night, a near-black console — must not be lifted to a mid grey. A **cutout** subject is toned to L\* 62 ± 4, because it will sit on paper with dark ink beside it. A **plate** gets the clip and contrast guards plus the edge guard, with the mean-luminance target applied as a **soft pull of at most ±10 L\* toward 62**, never a hard set. Both are design judgement. Every applied coefficient is written to the sidecar, so the transform is auditable — which matters in the spirit of CAP 3.7, where documentary evidence for objective claims must be held before publication, and knowing exactly what was done to the image of the prize is part of that.

**The counter chip's footprint.** §5.9 overlays a paper chip on the photo well at its top-left. The chip is opaque, so the only legibility question is whether its 1px `--rule` border reads against what is behind it. §5 declares that chip rect to the normaliser the way it already declares its exclusion rects to §8 — §9 publishes no coordinates of its own and moves with §5 automatically — and the normaliser records the mean L\* and σ of the declared rect in well-relative coordinates and hands them over in the sidecar. What §5 does with a near-paper reading there is §5's rule, not this section's.

**Tooling, and the constraint it places on the whole spec.** `sharp`, `jimp` and `canvas` are absent: VERIFIED in-session, `package.json` lists exactly two dependencies, `cheerio` and `playwright`. Two engines are actually present — Chromium canvas inside `page.evaluate` (the repo's existing idiom; `freehero.mjs:20-33` already does downscale-and-composite work this way, and `publish.mjs:57-67` already round-trips a PNG through a canvas to JPEG) and ffmpeg/ffprobe, confirmed present at `/opt/homebrew/bin` and already hardcoded at `encode.mjs:2` (`-vf signalstats` yields YAVG/YLOW/YHIGH; `eq=gamma=…:contrast=…:saturation=…` applies). **Recommend Chromium canvas as primary**, because `fetchimg.mjs:173` already launches one shared browser for the whole run and because computing the histogram and applying the transform in the same JavaScript keeps both in the sidecar. ffmpeg is the fallback and the right engine for any master that must also serve as a video frame.

§9's own analysis budget is bounded and should be stated so it is not confused with an open-ended image-analysis subsystem: histograms and ring statistics at 64–512 px on **one** candidate per draw in the expected case (§9.10), which is tens of small decodes per run. Any other section proposing per-pixel image analysis inherits this same two-dependency constraint and must make its own tooling decision against it; §8.8's parity gate is the case in point, and it is §8's to resolve, not this section's.

**Timeout discipline.** `fetchimg.mjs`'s own header names "hard per-draw timeout (never hangs — see the @imgly lesson)" as a design rule, and `downloadImage` enforces a 15s abort. The normaliser inherits the same rule: a hard per-candidate budget, and a failure is a refusal, never a hang. Without this, an ingest stage in front of an already-stalled pipeline becomes the new stall.

---

### 9.7 Tier 2 — the two semantic failures (probabilistic, two engines)

The research names three failures: marketing collages with baked-in text, WAF block pages, and branded info-cards. Block pages are Tier 0. The other two are semantic and need a probabilistic tier.

**Deterministic pre-filter (high recall, low precision by design).**

*Baked-in text.* No OCR exists in the repo — no tesseract, no OCR package, no vision API beyond Gemini. The pre-filter is a stroke-density detector: downsample to 512px long edge, compute a luminance gradient, count connected horizontal runs of high-gradient pixels 8–60px tall with row occupancy above 35%. Text lines produce dense, horizontally aligned, evenly spaced gradient bands. Two or more such bands, or one band wider than 40% of the frame, marks the asset suspect. Any band it finds is also recorded in the sidecar, because §9.4's L-notch test needs it.

*Collage / info-card.* Four signals; any two mark the asset suspect:
- a single dominant colour within ΔE 3 covering ≥35% of pixels (a poster ground, not a photograph);
- that dominant colour having C\* > 60 with ≥25% coverage (the darts tile's red, the Xbox tile's green);
- a high-saturation near-circular blob 8–20% of frame diameter in a corner quadrant (the red "NEW" rosette, the red "Buy 10 Get 2 Free" roundel — both present in the rendered mockup);
- ≥3 disjoint subject clusters after background keying, each >4% of frame.

**Adjudicator.** Only pre-filter suspects go to Gemini. `GOOGLE_GENERATIVE_AI_API_KEY` is present in `~/pdd-aggregator/.env` (verified in-session) and `aihero.mjs:16-27` already calls `generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta`, so there is no new plumbing. The call returns strict JSON: `{ has_text, text_content, is_collage, is_block_page, has_promo_badge, subject, confidence }`. Volume is bounded by §9.10's stop-at-first-admitted rule: `N + ⌈N/2⌉` images a day in the expected case at §5.11's deck size `N`, five times that at worst, and only the suspects among them.

**Confidence handling follows the repo's own precedent exactly.** `apply-vision.mjs:21-28` refuses to auto-apply any result whose `confidence` is `"low"`, and `apply-vision.mjs:39-41` writes those to a manual-review file (`~/Desktop/pdd-draft-low-confidence.json`) instead. Mirror it: `high` and `medium` verdicts decide automatically; `low` neither accepts nor refuses and falls to Tier 3.

**A composite verdict demotes, never drops.** It enters §9.4's refusal ladder at the next candidate. This is what makes the precision weakness affordable: a false positive on a legitimate bold-ground studio shot (the Xbox tile is arguably exactly that) costs a better-looking photo, not a missing slide.

**Honest limits.** Gemini is non-deterministic and will disagree with itself across runs. It is a per-image cost. It sends third-party operator photography to a third-party API, which is a data-handling decision the daily routine has not made before for images. And the pre-filter's precision is its weak point, not its recall.

---

### 9.8 Tier 3 — human and Claude QA, and what it costs in operator minutes

`DAILY.md:50-57` already specifies a single composite QA pass in which Claude reviews `contact.mjs`'s contact sheet — every fetched candidate for every draw, tiled at 200 × 200 with `object-fit: contain` on white (contact.mjs:36-37) — and confirms each `pick.txt` chose "the cleanest, no-rival-branding shot", swapping a pick or a whole draw where a page came back blocked or branded. **This tier adds no new pass.** It is that pass, improved in two ways:

1. The sheet shows the **normalised master, large**, with the rejected raw candidates small beside it and each one's refusal tier and reason printed, so the reviewer judges what will actually ship and can see why the others did not.
2. A Tier-3 rejection is **persistent** (§9.10). Today the judgement dies with the archive.

**The time budget, because nobody in this spec has totalled the minutes it is adding.** The sheet has one row per draw fetched, which is `N + ⌈N/2⌉` at §5.11's deck size `N` — twelve rows at §5.11's current constant, against five fetched today. One master at 420 px plus its rejected raws at 120 px is one row; at roughly 20 seconds a row to form a judgement, the image step is **≤ 4 minutes a day** and scales linearly with `N`. The governing rule is that the sheet is one scroll or the sheet is wrong: if a reviewer has to hunt, the layout is the defect, not the reviewer. §12 owns the whole-day operator budget; this is §9's line item in it, stated so it can be added up.

Tier 3 remains a judgement call, not a code assert, consistent with how DAILY.md:59-60 already frames its gates ("Claude visual judgement calls, not code asserts unless noted").

---

### 9.9 What is not automatable here, stated plainly

- **Reliable OCR.** Not present and not installable within the stated tooling. "Delete the baked-in text and keep the photograph" is not available deterministically.
- **Generative cleanup.** `carousel/aihero.mjs` already attempts precisely this: its prompt instructs Gemini to "Remove ALL text, logos, watermarks, price tags, badges, ticket prices, confetti, people and any busy/branded background from the original" and re-render on a near-black studio backdrop (aihero.mjs:8-11). **It must stay out of the daily path.** It replaces the photograph of the prize with a generated image of the prize, which fails CAP's requirement that promotional material not create a false overall impression, and sits directly in the line of Instagram's Recommendation Guidelines exclusion for "unoriginal content that is largely repurposed from another source". Its default backdrop (#0d0d0f, aihero.mjs:10) is also the rejected dark register. This is named explicitly because it is the obvious thing to reach for and it is wrong.
- **Perfect cutouts.** `freehero.mjs` runs `@imgly/background-removal` inside Chromium with no API key, and its own header states the caveat: it "removes the BACKGROUND only; text/logos baked into a flat marketing collage are not erased" (freehero.mjs:3-4). It also poisons the process — a subsequent browser's `setContent` hangs for 60s (freehero.mjs:6-9) — and must stay in the isolated subprocess `build.mjs:95-98` already spawns. It only runs today under `CARD=cutout`, which is not the default (build.mjs:43). It is useful where the deterministic luminance key already works and useless on a composite, which is why the cutout path uses the key instead.
- **Judging whether the photo shows the advertised prize.** Semantic, and out of scope here. That belongs with the existing grand-prize vision QA (`apply-vision.mjs`).

---

### 9.10 Cache and invalidation

**There is no cache today.** `.fetched/` lives inside `~/Desktop/pdd-today/` (config.json:8), and `plan.mjs:17-32` archives the entire previous working directory into `archive/<date>-<ms>/`, pruning past `archiveDays: 14` (config.json:9). Every day re-fetches and reprocesses from zero, including for a draw seen last week, and every QA correction to `pick.txt` is discarded with the archive. This section is §12's answer to its own **Q13** ("Where do normalised image derivatives live, and what deletes them?"): option (c), local disk, plus a repo-tracked rejects file.

**Content-addressed store.**

- **Location:** `~/.pdd-assets/`, overridable by `PDD_ASSETS` in the same way `PDD_DIR` overrides the working directory at `config.mjs:21-23`. It must sit **outside** `pdd-today/`, because `plan.mjs:21` sweeps everything in the working directory except `archive` into the archive folder.
- **Key:** `sha256(sourceBytes) + ":" + NORMALISER_VERSION`, truncated to 16 hex characters. Content-addressed, so a re-fetch of identical bytes is a hit regardless of URL, and a normaliser change invalidates the whole store without a manual purge.
- **Contents per key:** `plate.jpg` and/or `cutout.png`, plus `meta.json` recording source URL, source sha256, fetched-at ISO timestamp, decoded source dimensions, the subject bounding box, any detected text bands, the stored plate size, per-surface eligibility, every applied transform with its numeric coefficients, the edge-guard measurements, the chip-footprint statistics, the Tier-2 verdict with its engine name and confidence, and the Tier-3 decision where one was made.

**One candidate is normalised, not five.** The normaliser walks candidates in `fetchimg.mjs`'s existing rank order and **stops at the first that is admitted**. The worst case is the five that `fetchimg.mjs:165` fetches; the expected case is near one. This is what keeps both the Tier-2 bill and the Tier-3 sheet bounded, and it is the difference between normalising `5 × (N + ⌈N/2⌉)` images a day and normalising `N + ⌈N/2⌉`.

**Four invalidation triggers, all explicit:**

| Trigger | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Normaliser version bump | in the key — global and automatic |
| Source bytes changed | in the key — automatic |
| Operator swapped the photo without changing the draw | the pointer `draw_slug → key` is stored separately with a 14-day TTL matching `archiveDays`; on expiry the source URL is re-fetched and re-hashed. Identical bytes cost one HTTP request and no reprocessing |
| Manual rejection | Tier 3 retires that key permanently (see below) |

**Rejections do not live in the cache.** The draft of this design put them in the sidecar, which contradicts disposability: a purged or lost cache would silently resurrect every rejected asset. Decision: a Tier-3 rejection is appended to a repo-tracked `carousel/asset-rejects.json` — `{ sha256, reason, date }` — which the normaliser consults before selecting any key. It is small, it survives a cache wipe and a move to a cloud runner, it needs no database round-trip, and it is reviewable in a diff. The sidecar keeps a copy for audit only.

**Disposability.** Deleting `~/.pdd-assets/` must cost nothing but reprocessing time. No unique state may exist only there. It is not the Supabase `carousel-slides` bucket (config.json:7), and `cleanup.mjs` — which frees `{date}/{slug}/` objects once every `carousel_posts` row for the day is terminal (cleanup.mjs:26-30, 78-90) — must not touch it.

**Size, re-derived against §5.11's deck size (my arithmetic, not measured).** This supersedes the ~500 KB-per-key figure §5.11's own ruling used when it sized this section: that figure predates the 1600 × 2000 plate cap and the alpha cutout. A plate at up to 1600 × 2000 in JPEG q90 is roughly 450–850 KB; take 650 KB. A 1200 × 1200 cutout PNG with alpha is roughly 0.7–1.6 MB; take 1.0 MB, and take 40% as an unmeasured planning figure for the share of admitted assets that yield one (open question 8). Mean per key ≈ 650 KB + 0.4 × 1.0 MB = **1.05 MB**.

The daily path touches `N + ⌈N/2⌉` draws — `fetchimg.mjs:165-170` already fetches exactly that set, so no code change is needed to scale it — with one candidate normalised per draw in the expected case and five in the worst. At §5.11's current constant that is **12 keys a day expected, 60 worst case**. With the 14-day pointer TTL the steady state is 14 × 12 ≈ 168 keys ≈ **176 MB** expected and 14 × 60 = 840 keys ≈ **882 MB** worst case — both inside the **2 GB LRU bound**, which therefore survives the deck going from five draws to eight and does not need reopening. Normalising the entire enterable corpus would be roughly 899 × 1.05 MB ≈ **944 MB**, carrying §12.3's own caveat on that count: 899 is a 2026-09-17 snapshot that moves daily and does not reconcile with its own category breakdown (897).

---

### 9.11 What normalisation fixes, measured on the mockup

The draft argued this through the cover thumbnail strip. **The strip is deleted** — §5.15 removes `thumbsHtml()` (render.mjs:126-131 definition, render.mjs:153 call site) and §5.4 states "No photograph. No thumbnail strip." — so the argument is re-pointed at the surfaces that survive. The measurement is kept, because it is the best evidence in the section and it was never really about tiles: it is a sample of what operator photography contains.

**The retired strip's geometry, kept as the retrospective case for deleting it.** `.intro-wrap` carried `padding: 96px 54px 132px` (styles.css:389-390), leaving 972 CSS px of content width; `.thumbs` was `width: 100%; gap: 14px` (styles.css:398) and each `.thumb` was `flex: 1 1 0; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1` (styles.css:399), so at 5 draws each tile was (972 − 4×14)/5 = **183 CSS px** and at 6 draws (972 − 5×14)/6 = **150 CSS px**. At §5.11's deck size the strip would be (972 − 7×14)/8 = **109.25 CSS px** per tile, which at the profile-grid scale DAILY.md:69-70 gates against is **17.4 px** — the grid's 3:4 centre-crop maps 1012.5 CSS px onto ~161 px, a **0.159×** scale. That is what makes the deletion final rather than a matter of taste: the strip does not survive the deck it would have to serve. `.thumb-photo img { object-fit: cover }` (styles.css:403) hard-cropped whatever arrived, and the strip's only normalisation was decorative — a 2px accent border, a radial accent-tinted background and three box-shadows (styles.css:399-402), all of which go with it. (§5.11's ruling also strikes the draft's second consequence — that the strip could grow upward into the band of uniform paper measured on the mockup at rows 1404–2158 of 2700, 754 px, 27.9% of cover height — because the strip no longer exists to be given that job. The measurement is recorded here only so nobody re-derives it.)

**Measured on the approved mockup** (`~/Desktop/pdd-directions/D-merged-01-cover.png`, confirmed 2160 × 2700 by ffprobe, inspected in-session; sample = 1 rendered cover, 6 tiles):

| # | Tile | Baked-in text | Promo furniture | Ground |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Samsung watch | "SAMSUNG" wordmark | red "NEW" starburst | peach/cream gradient |
| 2 | DJI Avata 360 | "dji / AVATA 360 / MOTION FLY MORE COMBO / includes Goggles N2" | — | villa/pool photography |
| 3 | iPhone 17 Pro | "IPHONE 17 PRO & AIRPODS PRO 3" + Apple mark | — | white with lilac gradient |
| 4 | Xbox Series X | "1TB SERIES X" + Xbox mark | — | flat saturated green |
| 5 | Darts setup | "THE ULTIMATE DARTS SETUP" — **and `object-fit: cover` had already clipped it to "HE ULTIMAT"** | "+ INSTANT WINS" banner, cut-out human figure | saturated red |
| 6 | iPhone 18 Pro Max | "Win iPhone 18 Pro Max" | red "Buy 10 Get 2 Free" roundel | near-black with gold |

Six of six carry baked-in text, and on tile 5 the existing crop had already amputated the first letter of two lines of it. Two carry a competing promotional badge — one of which, "Buy 10 Get 2 Free", is another operator's live offer being republished on a PDD surface. One is a full collage with a cut-out figure. Six grounds, no two alike. Two also trip observed category clichés directly: the red "NEW" rosette and the "Buy 10 Get 2 Free" roundel are retail-sticker vocabulary, and the set as a whole is "inheriting operator artwork unfiltered", which the teardown observed at CompWatch, ThePrizeFinder and PDD's own `/draws` grid.

**Where that evidence now lands.** The same six images, unnormalised, would be:

1. **The Reel's whole frame.** §6.3 puts the photograph at 86.406% of the frame during the open window and never below its floor, with no card frame to hide a crop behind. At tile 5's density, an ungraded collage is not a backdrop to the Reel; it is the Reel. This is the strongest form of §9's case and it did not exist before §6.2 deleted `.pcard`.
2. **The carousel's largest single element.** §5.7 makes the photo well the flexible block and the biggest thing on a draw slide. A slide whose photograph shouts "THE ULTIMATE DARTS SETUP / + INSTANT WINS" is not PDD's slide.
3. **The sheet edge, on every draw slide.** §5.9 puts the *next* draw's photograph in a 96 px slice. A slice of a saturated red collage reads as a colour bar, not as paper; a slice of a normalised plate reads as the next sheet in the stack, which is the entire cue.
4. **The Story's band 3 crop.** §7.2 calls this the most demanding frame and says so itself: a 3.48:1 slice of an unnormalised operator marketing collage is unreadable.

**The chrome becomes deletable, which is worth stating beyond the strip.** The blurred-self backdrops, the `.contain` padding and the `.photo-grad` inset shadow exist to hold together images that no longer need holding together. Deleting them rather than restyling them serves the Verizon Media/Publicis finding (5,616 US adults, fielded April 2019) of −12% ad memory when logos crowd the screen alongside captions, and the derived rule "delete chrome rather than shrink type". Carry that study's caveat: it is a single 2019 US ad-memory study, not a measurement of this account.

**On Instagram's second-chance behaviour.** Mosseri (Oct 2024) states that when a viewer does not swipe, Instagram "will often give that carousel a second chance and automatically move to that second piece of media". The draft attached §9's case to that slide. Which slide carries the first photograph is §5.6's to set, and the rulings in play disagree: §5.11's dot-grid ruling makes slide 2 the count slide with no photograph and moves §5.6 Delta 3's image-quality gate to slide 3, while the C2/C16 ruling keeps a photo well on every draw slide. §9's gate binds wherever the first photograph lands. Stated honestly: on the dot-grid ruling, slide 1 and slide 2 both carry no photograph, and the second-chance argument stops being an asset-quality argument at all — §9's case then rests on the Reel and on the profile-grid cover instead. That is a weaker version of the claim than the draft made and it is the accurate one.

**And the tension §2 named is real.** §2 observes that inner slides must be distinguishable at thumbnail size and that normalising to a uniform crop and ground makes them look *more* alike. The resolution is that this stage removes **incidental** variance — ground colour, tone, aspect, another operator's baked-in text — and preserves **subject** variance, which is the only differentiator §2 accepts anyway ("the differentiator must be the data … not the photo treatment"). Six identical grounds with six different prizes on them is more distinguishable at the ~24 px the retired strip's tiles reached in the profile grid than six different grounds with six unreadable captions.

---

### 9.12 Per-prize accent derived from the photograph

The option: extract a dominant colour from each normalised master and use it as a per-draw accent on a rule, tile edge or figure.

**Recommendation: do not build this.** Four reasons:

1. **Colour is semantic in the approved system, and hierarchy is a compliance surface.** Verdict green, caution red and signal amber are all reserved by §3 for specific meanings, and per-category visual identity is §8's — §9 adds none of its own. CAP's guidance is verbatim that "the page design, layout or format of the promotion" must not be misleading and that promoters "should not embolden or otherwise emphasise claims to create an overall impression that is not true". An arbitrary photo-derived hue landing near verdict green on a draw whose facts were not checked is precisely that failure.
2. **The derived colour is the operator's.** A composite is refused, but a plate still carries the operator's art direction. Deriving PDD's accent from it hands the operator's brand colour a slot in PDD's layout — the same "inherit operator artwork unfiltered" failure §9.11 measures, just laundered through a colour picker.
3. **It works against the only uncontested position available.** The approved direction rests on §2.3's unoccupied territories — #1, the light ground, and #5, numerals as the only ornament — with one restrained accent as its whole identity. A palette that changes per draw is the opposite of a recognisable identity, and at ~66 followers recognition is the scarce asset.
4. **The architecture makes it expensive.** `reel-template.mjs:46`, `story.mjs:31` and `reel.mjs:69` build their CSS by scraping `/(?:^|\n)\s*(?::root|\[data-theme="[^"]+"\])\s*\{[^}]*\}/g` out of `styles.css`. Only `:root` and `[data-theme="x"]` token blocks propagate — reel-template.mjs:41-43 says so in a comment, "Descendant rules are intentionally skipped". A per-draw accent is not a theme token, so it would have to be injected as an inline style separately on each of the three surfaces — more machinery for a worse result.

**Build this instead, because it is cheap and genuinely useful:** the normaliser stores the master's mean luminance and whether the subject reads light or dark against its ground. The renderer then picks between the two already-defined ink tones deterministically rather than by guessing. That is a legibility decision, not a brand-colour decision, and it is the honest version of "derive something from the photo".

---

### 9.13 Three different things in this spec are called "normalisation"

A builder reading across sections will conflate them, so they are named here once:

- **Asset normalisation** — operator photography, this section, the image path (`fetchimg.mjs`, `imgcheck.mjs`, the new `normalise.mjs`).
- **Title normalisation** — the prize string. §6.3's Row B character cap and §6's own open question about "the ingest-time normaliser" are about text, and the contract is §5.12's `cleanTitle()` rules, with the permitted-wording law at §10.6a. §9 owns only the *placement* of the second-person and comparative strip — it runs at the aggregator's text ingest, upstream of selection, so §5.12's swap rule is a backstop that rarely fires — and restates none of the wording.
- **Figure provenance** — `total_entries` and its source URL, read time and extraction method. That contract is **§10.4's**, sequenced as Stage 0 of §12.4, and this section defines none of it, including its column names. The image sidecar's provenance and the figure provenance are separate artefacts with separate lifecycles: one lives in a disposable cache, the other in the `draws` row.

---

### 9.14 Measurement honesty

This section's effect cannot be measured at the asset level and should not be claimed to be. Carousel children have no individual insights in the Graph API — only the parent album object carries metrics — so there is no per-slide, swipe, exit-rate or completion figure in the API or the app. `carousel/insights.mjs` `mapPayload()` (insights.mjs:21) ingests only likes and comments from `ig_media`, account reach from `ig_reach`, and the three Facebook counters; it pulls no saves, no Instagram shares, no views and no watch time. And the baseline is 12 rows in `carousel_posts` spanning 2026-06-29 to 2026-07-03, with the pipeline dark since.

So the only honest judgement available is post-level accounts-reached over a run of posts, against a baseline that does not yet exist. Normalisation should be argued on what it demonstrably removes — another operator's promotional text from PDD's surfaces, five separate blurred copies of an operator's colours, an unreadable slice of a collage in Story band 3, and a 1080 × 1920 Reel frame that is someone else's poster — not on a reach number.

Also excluded deliberately: the "first slide carries 80% of the weight" claim, which the digest marks as having no source. The case here rests on Mosseri's published second-chance behaviour, on §6.3's own frame arithmetic and on the profile-grid crop geometry, all of which are documented, not on any weighting folklore.

---

### Decisions this section commits to
- §9 is the sole normative owner of asset normalisation. A normalisation stage (`carousel/normalise.mjs`) sits between `fetchimg.mjs` and the three renderers; `build.mjs`, `reel.mjs` and `story.mjs` all consume it, replacing their three independent `minDimOk(auto,500)` calls at build.mjs:63, reel.mjs:219 and story.mjs:236.
- `pick.txt` becomes `pick.json` carrying `{ key, plate, cutout, eligible{well,sheetEdge,reel,story}, rejected[] }`; the three read sites that change are build.mjs:47-53, reel.mjs:205-211 and story.mjs:223-229.
- The contract guarantees a known ground, tone, subject box and per-surface minimum resolution — NOT a single aspect ratio. The draft's "the widest aspect anything needs is 1.341:1" is withdrawn: the surviving surfaces need crops from 0.0958:1 (the §5.9 sheet edge) to 3.48:1 (§7.2's band 3, 950 × 273), a 36:1 spread.
- The contract no longer promises a typographic fallback. DAILY.md:57's "fall back to a clean typographic card" is superseded: a refused asset becomes a §10.8 class-B drop entering §5.11's ladder, and the typographic card survives only as a §5 layout state.
- Master geometry is re-derived at shipped pixels from the surfaces the spec ships — §6.2's full-bleed 1080×1920 Reel, §5.7's 1015-wide photo well, §5.9's 96×1002 sheet edge and §7.2's 950-wide band 3 — not from `.card`, `.pcard` or the deleted thumbnail strip. The binding demands are **1920 px of height** (the Reel) and **1353 px of width** under §7.6's optional 1440×1800 Facebook variant, falling to the Reel's own **1080 px** without it.
- Two derivatives, letters retired to avoid collision with §7.9's Meta policy Classes A and B. The **plate**: JPEG q90 on the source's own aspect, largest rectangle within the 1.35× budget, capped at 1600 × 2000 (1536 × 1920 is what the Reel's pan allowance asks for; the cap also clears the 1353 px width demand by 247 px and the 1920 px height demand by 80 px). The **cutout**: 1200 × 1200 PNG, alpha preserved and no ground baked in, subject in a centred 1100 × 1100 box.
- Surface map: photo well and Story band 3 take the cutout when one exists, else the plate; the Reel, the Reel cover and the sheet edge take the **plate only**. The Reel never takes a cutout, because the entire 1100 px subject box is 1,210,000 px² = 58.4% of a 1080×1920 frame, below §6.3's 71.563% photograph floor (1,483,970 px²), so a cutout would discharge that floor with paper.
- Resolution floors replace `max(w,h) >= 500`, each hard floor being ⌈preferred ÷ 1.35⌉: plate-full ≥1536×1920 / ≥1138×1423; plate still-only ≥1015×1002 / ≥752×743, rising to ≥1353×1336 / ≥1003×990 if §7.6's optional Facebook variant is taken; cutout subject short edge ≥1100 / ≥815. A source between 1080×1920 and the full tier's width floor is tried at zero pan rather than failed, so a no-upscale source is never rejected in favour of a worse one. Both floors ship behind `ASSET_MIN_PLATE` and `ASSET_MIN_SUBJECT` so open question 1 can retune them without a code change.
- Source aspect outside 1:3 to 3:1 is refused, closing the banner-strip hole the longest-edge gate leaves open. imgcheck.mjs:36 reverses: an undecodable buffer is refused, not passed — the render gate does not judge resolution (render.mjs:20-27 waits only on fonts and image load/error, render.mjs:191 on `window.__ready`), so the comment's premise is false.
- §6's L-notch constraint is honoured as an intersection test: the Reel crop is valid only if neither the subject box nor any detected text band intersects x 853…1080 × y 1152…1920 (227 × 768 = 174,336 px², 8.41% of frame); the crop pans within the available slack (456 px from a full-size plate) and refuses if no placement works.
- One refusal ladder, and §9 reaches §5.11's backup pool last: next candidate → the operator's stored `image_url` → the still-only tier (if only the Reel floor failed) → refuse, at which point the draw becomes a §10.8 class-B drop entering §5.11's ladder. §9 consumes at most one backup per draw.
- The 2px `#D8D3C8` hairline and 2% inset around a photograph are DELETED: §5.7 forbids a border, §5.14 makes the token decorative-only, and the Reel's full-bleed frame could not carry one anyway. Paper-adjacent legibility is handled by an edge guard instead — 95th-percentile L* ≤ 92 on the outer 24 px ring of any paper-abutting shipped crop, i.e. ≥4.6 L* below §3's paper at its computed L* 96.6 (Y = 0.9137, §8's published value). It is a test that steers the crop anchor, never a transform, and a failure is recorded as `edge_dissolves` rather than fixed with a vignette.
- The byte floor rises from 3000 (fetchimg.mjs:153) to 8192, plus a 64×64 frame-entropy test that runs ONLY on the trimmed region after the uniform border ring is removed, so a legitimate white-studio product shot is not eaten by its own low entropy. Both thresholds are design judgement.
- `fetchimg.mjs` adopts `looksBlocked()` (extractor.mjs:40) and `BLOCK_RE` (probe.mjs:27); `.fetched/report.json` distinguishes "blocked" from "no candidates". What this buys is naming the cause, since most challenge pages are already excluded by the content-type filter at fetchimg.mjs:149-151.
- Ground detection is the 8 px border ring: σ < 6/255 and mean L* > 88 yields a cutout (and a plate too, when the plate floor is met); σ ≥ 6 yields a plate only; a composite is refused.
- Tone targets are per-master: a cutout subject is toned to mean L* 62 ± 4; a plate gets the clip, contrast and edge guards plus a soft pull of at most ±10 L* toward 62, never a hard set, so a black car at night is not lifted to mid grey. Every coefficient is recorded in the sidecar.
- §5 declares the counter chip's rect to the normaliser the way it already declares exclusion rects to §8; §9 publishes no coordinates for it, records the mean L* and σ of that declared rect in well-relative coordinates, and hands the reading to §5. What §5 does about a near-paper reading is §5's rule.
- Chromium canvas is the primary tone/geometry engine (fetchimg.mjs:173 already launches one shared browser; publish.mjs:57-67 already round-trips images through one); ffmpeg at /opt/homebrew/bin, hardcoded at encode.mjs:2, is the fallback. VERIFIED: package.json has exactly two dependencies, cheerio and playwright — a constraint any section proposing per-pixel image analysis inherits and must answer for itself.
- The normaliser processes candidates in rank order and stops at the first admitted, so the expected cost is one master per draw and the worst case is fetchimg.mjs:165's five.
- Tier 2 runs a deterministic pre-filter (stroke-density text bands; four collage signals, any two) and sends only its suspects to Gemini for a strict-JSON verdict, reusing GOOGLE_GENERATIVE_AI_API_KEY (verified present in .env) and the v1beta endpoint already called at aihero.mjs:16-27. Confidence handling copies apply-vision.mjs:21-28 and :39-41: high and medium decide automatically, low falls to Tier 3.
- Tier 3 is not a new pass: it is DAILY.md:50-57's existing composite QA, with the master shown large beside its rejected raws and their reasons. Its budget is ≤4 minutes a day at §5.11's deck size — `N + ⌈N/2⌉` rows at ~20 seconds each — scaling linearly with N, and it is §9's line item in §12's operator-time total.
- aihero.mjs stays out of the daily path; @imgly background removal stays in the isolated subprocess (build.mjs:95-98, non-default CARD=cutout at build.mjs:43) and its own header (freehero.mjs:3-4) states it cannot erase baked-in text.
- The cache is content-addressed at ~/.pdd-assets/ (PDD_ASSETS override, mirroring config.mjs:21-23), keyed sha256(sourceBytes) + normaliser version, deliberately outside pdd-today/ so plan.mjs:21 cannot archive it. This is §12's Q13 answered: option (c), local disk.
- Tier-3 rejections do NOT live in the cache sidecar. They append to a repo-tracked carousel/asset-rejects.json keyed by source sha256 with a reason, so the cache stays genuinely disposable and a rejection survives a cache wipe or a move to a cloud runner.
- Four invalidation triggers: normaliser version bump, changed source bytes, a 14-day TTL on the draw_slug → key pointer, and a rejects-file entry that permanently retires a key. cleanup.mjs (cleanup.mjs:26-30, 78-90) must not touch the cache.
- Cache size re-derived against §5.11's deck size, superseding the ~500 KB/key figure §5.11's ruling used: (N + ⌈N/2⌉) draws a day × ~1 key each expected, 5 worst case, at ~1.05 MB a key (650 KB plate + 40% × 1.0 MB cutout) = ~176 MB expected and ~882 MB worst case at a 14-day TTL. The 2 GB LRU bound survives the deck growing and does not need reopening; the full corpus would be ~944 MB on §12.3's 899-draw snapshot, which §12.3 itself flags as a moving, unreconciled figure.
- The cover thumbnail strip argument is retired with the strip. The retired geometry is kept as its own retrospective justification: 183 px per tile at 5 draws, 150 px at 6, and (972 − 7×14)/8 = 109.25 CSS px at §5.11's deck size, which is 17.4 px at the 0.159× profile-grid scale DAILY.md:69-70 gates against (1012.5 CSS px mapped onto ~161 px). The mockup's six-tile measurement is kept and re-pointed at the Reel frame, the photo well, the sheet edge and Story band 3.
- Once ingest guarantees ground and tone, the render-time compensations are deleted in ALL FIVE places, not one: styles.css:313-314, reel-template.mjs:184-185, reel-template.mjs:168-169, reel.mjs:87-88 and story.mjs:79-80 (the blurred-self backdrops), plus build.mjs:117 framePhotoContain, styles.css:320 contain padding and styles.css:323-324 photo-grad. styles.css:399-402's `.thumb` chrome goes with the strip under §5.15 and needs no separate instruction.
- No per-prize accent is derived from the photograph. The normaliser instead stores mean luminance and light/dark subject polarity so the renderer picks deterministically between the two defined ink tones.
- §9 renders no age mark, no territory mark and no conditions wording anywhere. Those are §10.2's and this section restates none of them.

### Open questions
- The distribution of source image dimensions across the enterable corpus is unmeasured, so every floor here is geometry-derived rather than corpus-calibrated — and they are far stricter than the 500 px longest-edge rule they replace, above all the Reel's 1920 px height. The measurement that matters is the share of the corpus clearing the **full** (Reel) floor versus only the still-only floor. Restated as the gate §5.11 needs: does one category yield `drawsPerDeck + BACKUPS` usable candidates per run? This must be measured before §5.11's deck-size constant is locked, not after.
- Does the luminance key behave acceptably on products that are themselves white or near-white against a white studio ground (a white iPhone on white, a pale watch strap)? The key would eat the product edge, and the border-ring test cannot distinguish that case from a coloured product on white. A specular-highlight or edge-gradient guard may be needed, and §9.5's entropy fix does not solve this one.
- What is the current official per-image price and rate limit for the Gemini vision SKU used as the Tier-2 adjudicator, and does the account's tier retain submitted images for training? aihero.mjs:5 carries ~$0.039/img for gemini-2.5-flash-image as an unverified code comment, and a text-verdict model is a different SKU in any case. The retention question matters because the images are third-party operator photography.
- Should the plate be written back to Supabase so the site's /draws grid inherits the same treatment? The cache design would support it, but it is out of scope for the social template rework and would change site image egress, which memory records as already having caused two blowouts.
- How often does §9.4's still-only tier actually fire — that is, how often does a source clear the carousel's floor but not the Reel's, and how often does a source clear the Reel's resolution floor but fail the L-notch placement? Together those determine whether the Reel becomes the deck's binding constraint on which draws can be used at all.
- Is §7.6's optional 1440×1800 Facebook variant worth a one-third rise in the still-only floor (1015×1002 → 1353×1336)? §7.6 presents the variant as free; it is free in render time and not free in inventory. §7.6's call, on this section's arithmetic.
- The edge guard steers the crop anchor but cannot always pass. What proportion of plates end up with `edge_dissolves: true`, and at what measured L*? If it is common, §5.7's no-border rule is buying less than it costs and §5 should see the number before deciding.
- What share of admitted assets yield a cutout? The 40% used in §9.10's cache arithmetic is a planning figure with nothing behind it, and it also sizes the Tier-3 sheet.

### Risks
- **The Reel is now the binding image consumer and nothing has been measured against it.** §6.2's full-bleed 1080×1920 frame asks for 1920 px of subject-anchored height where the old `.pcard` asked for 950 px on a 952-wide box, and §6 states the exposure itself: at 86.406% of the frame during the open window, an ungraded collage is the reel. Every floor in §9.4 is arithmetic against a corpus nobody has queried.
- **The photograph-share constants §9 leans on are §6.3's own construction.** §6.3 publishes 71.563% / 86.406%, and its own caveat is that the figure is an area calculation of opaque chrome, not a read of Instagram's classifier, since Meta publishes no threshold or definition for "majority text". §9's conclusions are built to survive the constant moving, but nothing here validates it.
- The collage detector's precision is its weak point. A legitimate single-product studio shot on a bold brand ground — the Xbox Series X tile in the mockup is arguably exactly that — trips two of the four signals and would be refused. The demote-never-drop ladder bounds the damage to a worse photo, but a category like tech-giveaways, where brand-coloured product tiles are the norm, could lose most of its candidates.
- §9 is one of several consumers of the same backup pool, with two triggers of its own (composite refusal and resolution refusal). §9.4 undertakes to exhaust its internal ladder first and to take at most one backup per draw, but the priority order among all the consumers is §5.11's to set, and without one whichever runs first wins and the rest escalate.
- A plate built from a white-studio source fills the Reel with photographed white. It is a photograph by any pixel measure and it satisfies §6.3's area figure, which cannot tell the two apart — so the dominance argument can be technically discharged by a frame that is mostly empty. This is the case where the gap between an area calculation and what a classifier might count actually shows.
- The pipeline has been dark since 2026-07-03 and the two later runs (2026-07-10, 2026-07-14) built complete decks and were abandoned at the publish step, not at build. Adding an ingest stage in front of a publish problem risks extending the dark period rather than shortening it. Sequencing matters and is not this section's to decide.
- Gemini is non-deterministic, and the content-addressed cache pins the first verdict against those bytes. An early wrong verdict becomes sticky until the normaliser version bumps, and there is no per-key re-adjudication trigger short of a Tier-3 override.
- Content-addressing means the same photo reused across two draws shares one key, so a Tier-3 rejection made for a draw-specific reason — wrong prize shown, not bad image — permanently retires a perfectly good asset for every other draw too. `asset-rejects.json` therefore needs its reason field used and a review path, not just a sha.
- Deleting the blurred-self backdrops and the contain padding removes the safety net that currently lets any aspect render without visibly breaking. If the normaliser ever emits an unexpected crop, the card breaks rather than degrades. The renderer needs a hard assert that the master's stored size meets the surface's demand before it draws.
- The blurred-self backdrop exists five times across four files and only one is in styles.css. The other four are string literals inside the video templates, outside the token-lift regex, so a change made only to the stylesheet leaves the Reel and Story still importing operator colour while the carousel has stopped — the exact silent carousel-video divergence the repo documents at styles.css:295-305.
- **There is no SSIM harness to gate these deletions with.** The draft said "the same SSIM harness should gate these deletions". VERIFIED in-session: a case-insensitive grep for `ssim` across the repository (excluding `node_modules`) returns exactly one hit — the comment block at styles.css:295-305, which records the 0.979-against-a-0.997-noise-floor measurement as prose. There is no harness, no test and no script behind it. So the eight deletions across four files land with no automated regression check unless one is written, and §9.6's own two-dependency constraint applies to writing it. For v1 the honest gate is a before/after contact sheet plus a byte-level assert that each named selector is absent from all three rendered CSS strings — the Reel and Story included, since they build their CSS by scraping.
- freehero.mjs imports @imgly/background-removal from esm.sh at runtime (freehero.mjs:22). The version IS pinned (1.5.7), but there is no local copy and no SRI, so an unattended daily routine depends on a third-party CDN being up and serving the same bytes — and that WASM blob already has a documented process-poisoning failure mode.
- Tier 2's network round-trips and the canvas work land inside a routine whose own header treats hanging as the primary failure mode. If the per-candidate timeout discipline slips, normalisation becomes the new stall in front of an already-stalled publish step.
- ~/.pdd-assets/ lives on the user's Mac. If the carousel routine ever moves to a cloud runner — as the aggregator daily QA routine already has — the cache is lost and every master with it. Rejections survive that move via the repo-tracked file; the reprocessing cost and the 14-day pointer state do not.
- Tier 0's entropy test runs on the trimmed region, which fixes the white-studio false positive but introduces a dependency: the trim must run before the admissibility test, so a mis-trim on a low-contrast image can cascade into a wrongful refusal at the cheapest, least-reviewed tier.
- The Tier-3 budget of four minutes a day is my arithmetic on a sheet that has not been built. It is the cheapest thing in the spec to get wrong in the direction that matters, because the dormancy was a human-gate failure and this is a human gate.
